PADGATE.

West.Ev GUILD.—The Bev. W. Mellor presided over a fair attendance at the monthly devotional meeting of the Wesley Guild which was held on Monday evening. A paper was read by Mr. Bert Mason, of Fearnhead, on " Pastor Hai-liai a convert from heathenism to Christianity." This is a book which is being read by the me:abets of the Guild reading circle. Mr. Mason ' gave an excellent description of the life and character of the subject, and read copions extracts illustrative of the various points of his paper. SCHOLARS' EXCCRSION.—On Saturday the scholars in the upper standards of Padgate National School bad a trip to Miller's Dale and Buxton, a largo party mak;ng the journey. The children were in charge of Mr. Blackwell, and were also accompanied by Miss Grounds and Miss Bibby. The party detrained at Miller's Dttle station, and then undertook the lovely seven-mile-walk through Miller's Dale, Chee Dale, and Ashwood Dale, stopping at the waterfall and the Lovers' Leap en route. When Buxton was reached a short rest was made, and then Poole's Cavern was visited, after which the more adventurous climbed the hill to -Solomon's Temple. After tea the principal sights of the town were visited. Padgate was again reached at 10 p.m.

WIRRAL AND: BIRKENHEAD SHOW. THIS YEAR'S ARRANGEMENTS. The Council has now issued the prize schedule for the • annual show. which is to be held in the permanent Show-yard at Bebington on Wednesday and Thursday, July 19th and 19th, under the presidency of _Thomas Lonsdale, Esq., Hooton. A most representative list of classes has been arranged and handsome prizes are again offered for competition. Classes for Kerry cattle have been included this year for the first time, and tber Council hope, owners of this •beautiful variety will favour the Society by sending exhibits for competition. The handsome challenge cups, which vary in value from 3 to 100 guineas, will again be competed for, in addition to which a large number of the Society's - specially-designed gold and silver medals will be offered for competition in the machinery. implements and miscellaneous section. Ever up to date, the Council have included classes for wagons, tradesmen's vans, and • private cars, and trials will take place on each day of the show. A most extensive classification has been • offered for lice stock and ,dairy produce.. Tandem driving and horse-leaping competitions will take place in the large judging ring on each afternoon of the show in addition to which there will be a grand parade of the • prize-winning animals during the second day. Dogs, onitry, and pigeons are most generously catered for, and several challenge cups varying in value from 5 to 50 guineas are being offered in the Inst-named section for competition for the first time at this Society's show, in addition to which there are over 100 special prizes over and ab,.ve the c:ass prizes offered for competition, in addition to which the Kennel Club have granted nearly 50 championships. Acceding to the request of a number of fanciers, the Council has generously •provided a most representative • classification for rabbitc•and caviee. and a long list of special prizes for these interesting exhibits are included in the prize schedule. The,band of the Ist olunteer Battalion Cheshire: Regiment and the liirkenk.c.ad and District Postal Band will provide the music 013 each day of the show. The several railway companies are issuing cheap tickets from val.ous parts of Laticachire. Cheshire, and •North Wales.

The London Season.—Week ends grow longer and more universal, and hostesses areesperiencing considers able difficulty in arranging parties for the few evenings that people are in town. Friday generally sees a great exodus to the seaside, or country, the return journey frequently being put off until Tuesday. There appears to be a growing disinclination to spending the longest and hest days of the year in London. and many leading hostesses are this summer in residence and entertaining at one of their country seats, simply coming to town for Court and Society functions. Doubtless the motor is largely responsible for this state of affairs, which by the way the London tradesmen deeply deplore. Royal Residences.—The statement that she King has granted the ;le of the Stud House, Hampton Court Park, to Major and Lady Sarah Wilson, rehalls to mind the fact that many of the residences in what may be called the Royal loan collection, go begging as far es Royalties are concerned. White Lodge, Richmond Park, the home of the late Duke and Duchess of Tech, and the birthplace of Prince Edward of Wales ' • Pem- broke Lodge—also in Richmond Park—; and Kerr Cottage, the rural retreat of the late Duke of Cambridge, could all have been secured by almost any member of the Royal Family, but none were eager, some declining on the score of the too near attentions of the motor cats and the speculative builder, while others pointed out that they already possessed as many homes as they could suitably, maintain. Our Distinguished American Visitors.— Great interest has been evinced in the visit of Mr. and Mrs. Long- worth—the latter perhaps better known to fame as Miss Alice Roosevelt—who are now "doing Europe " as part of the programme of their Wedding tour. " Princess Allus " as she is affectionately termed in America, has never been in this country before, and few Royalties have ever-had a more brilliant reception than has been accorded to the popular daughter of President Roosevelt. Mr. and Mrs. Longworth are the guests of Mr. and Mrs. Whitelaw Reid, at the American Embassy, which for the time being has been quite the centre of the social world; the King being present at the dinner party which was one of several magnificent entertainments given in honour of the distinguished visitors. Mr. and Mrs. Longworth are not inaking a long stay, but *their programme includes a visit to Ascot. and American society will be very prominently represented at the fashionable race meet- ing. Mrs. Longworth dresses well, but carefully refrains from exaggerated styles. She is of medium height, and her appearance suggests high intellectual gifts rather than any pronounced form of beauty. She is twelve years younger than her husband, whoni,accord- ing to American ideas, she married as much for his sterling merits as for his charming manners and musical gifts. The Empress Eugenies Modist idea of Dress.—The Empress Eugenie. who once reigned over the most brilliant Court iR Europe, has made the astonishing admissian to an American lady, that on only three occasions in her life has she worn a dress that cost as much as forty guineas. Of these one was her wedding dress.and another was the dress she wore at the baptism of tho Prince Imperial. Yet she was supposed to set the fashions, in which Paris, even more so ,than now, was the guiding spirit for the whole fashionable world. Now-a-days nothing is thought of paying forty guineas, or twice as much, for a dress even on an ordinary occa- sion, and although the Empress refers to a time before the age of luxury, and extravagance, which distin- guishes the present day, yet it is surprising to learn that she was able to reconcile such modest ideas of ' dress with her exalted position on the throne of France. The Crusade against the " Peek-a-boo " Blouse.— In America, both press and pulpit are enveighing against 11 the feminine craze for diaphanous summer clothing, I and especially against what in the elegance of American language is called the "peek-a-boo " blouse. One would think that" peep-o-day " *mad be a more appro- priate name, but wherever they got the word from the ' peek-a-boo" garment is being denounced by the " purity " organisation and it was reported that one minister was so moved to indignation that he told some members of his congregation that his churc)e was not a bathing establishment, and if thel could 'not come more suitably attired they had better stay at home. Some of the commerical firms too, are also interfering in the matter, and the New York Telephone Exchange has forbidden its girls to come to work in "indelicate" garments. The American girl has very independent notions, and it is doubtful whether such coercive measures will have much effect. It was found by our own enthusiasts that the transparent blouse was any- thing but comfortable in the hot sun, whilst risky in the cold and wet weather, and it is astonishing that this experience has not led to its being cast aside in America as, happily, it has been here. 7 Short Skirts.—With regard to the 'short skirt, tailors and dressmakers are excessively tisesome this summer. These worthy people raise every possible objection to the mode, and even when they finally agree to allow a skirt to clear the ground, it invariably mysteriously lengthens in the making. For all save dressy occasions, and of course evening wear, the short skirt should however, be insisted upon by the outdoar girl and woman, one is always sweeter tempered, and there- fore happier, when not anxious about skirt edges. More- over it is quite possible, despite all that has been, and is said, to the contrary for the short girl to wear the abbreviated skirt, and yet look well. The tall figure often means the big foot, while the shorter build fre- quently goes with pretty feet, which may confidently display themselves ankle high, and quite atone for the seeming shortening of the whole figures ' The Cure of Consampt,on.—When the Finsen light II treatment was first introduced in the London hospitals, I for which the Queen was largely instrumental, it was believed that it would prove to. be a complete cure for lnpus. Those expectations have not been altogether realised, for whilst it cares in some cases, in others it has no effect. It depends, it is said, upon the patient's own power of resisting the disease, and in those iry which this is weak, as fast as the light ceres, there is renewed infection. It is now however,announced, under what appears to be official authority, that a new dis- covery has been made by which the patient's power of ' resisting the disease is greatly strengthened, and a cure ; can then be effected. This raises sanguine ideas that before long that dread disease consumption will he euccessfully combated, for it is the same germ that causes lupus in one person, as gives rise to consumption of the lungs in another. If therefore the disease is susceptible to this new treatment in one case, there is strong probability that it will be so in the other, and great hopes are entertained that this fresh discovery will prove to he the means by which it will be possible to stamp out-consumption. Blundell took the remaining Guides and half the Gobikhas and faced the JilL Billy and los men got a gun in position, but could not fire until a word shouted across the rock torrent sent till retreating advance guard to the right, where, partially sheltered by some rocks/ they kept up a steady fire on the enemy. But the Gulistanis Isere in such great strength, that Briggs almost believed them when they yelled insultingly that they had cut up Rawson and his men, and would shortly do. the same to every Kaffir of an English- man, and the renegadex and other ICaffirs they had brought with them. It looked as if their peculiarly encouraging anatomical remarks might yet be made good in rough post-tnortenis, for though the Sikhs got across , the river,- they were exposed to a tremendous fire and lost heavily while doing it. The Colonel soon saw that perhaps it was a mistake to have sent them, for the two guns now in action made little impression on a rocky hill, where not an enemy could be seen- or even be known to be there, till the rifle spoke. And below the shoot the river was deeper. The' Sikhs took what shelter they could and fired steadily, but now Briggs wished they were back. He looked up at Blundell, and saw him half-way to the head of the shoot, his Pathan& and Goorkhas climbing like goats. Yes, they were almost up, and yeta moving torrent of rocks was between them and their obiective. He saw many of the Goorkhas fall as the Gulistanis fired, and then he saw them swerve away to the right with Blundell running on an easier slope. What .were they doing? For the Gulistanis•shouted-as though they had already won the day, and exposing themselves again hurled more rocks into the shoot. In two minutes Briggslost sight of all the Goorkhas, save those • who were wounded. But when he looked again he saw the enemy running towards Blundell, and the Goorkhas, who were above and behind them, on the right side of the shoot. They had cut off retreat by the one lofty mountain path. For when Blundell caught his breath 'again after that awful climb he saw that even there it was impossible to cross the rock slide, and they must go higher 'yet.. The only possible way' was to the right, and, running like a deer, he found a way and plunged into Ithe sharp, shaly stones half to his knees ' and Was over first. His meh came after him, each one crossing at a higher place, for they set the shoot moving and though it was narrow now it was still more dangerous than the icy torrent of a glacier. "Come 'on," he cried, and then he ran ahead and found the Gulistanis, who were just,too late to ,guard the path by which they had come and by which they must go; if they Went at all: They • were in a trap, And yet they were Many, and Blundell's men now no more than seventy. He WA left thirty on the way up. A Gulistani was within ten yards of him. Before he could raise hie -rifle Blundell was on him, and ran him through. But Blundell stayed and bade the men lie down.. Theirs was the advantage now, and every tribesman who shewed Was bowled over. They kept close behind their rocks, but the Guides and Goorkhas crawled ahead and spread a little, and saw where the brown,of them was,and fired into it, chuckling, and when' the Gulistanis saw how it was they cowered for a moment, and then raised a yell and rushed straight at them, tleir only chance. ." Hurrah . ' cried Blundell, and the next moment 'he was in as thick jammed mass of men. The Goorkhas smelt blood, and Were on fire, but , the Gulistanis were desperate and fought well. Blundell at first could get at no one, he forind his men round him. Even at their saVagest they thought of , the English officer as they always will. What Goorkha c‘n go back to his regiment if his officers are dead and ,he survives? But soon the press lessened, and his blood was up too, as savage as anyone's. What was going on down below, and what of Rawson, and what of England and England's honour and the good fights of old? In the middle of the hot, fierce joy of it he saw a girl's face just for a moment, and struck for her. The Gulistanis lay thick, but others pressed over them and, ight- ins- on the verge of the Stone shoot, many were driven into it and rolled headlong, and were cut to pieces aosain in the grinding null of sliding stone. Blundell stumbled over a dying Guide, and fell prone on a live Goorklia who had ,slipped in blood, and, rising, fell once more, into the hands of a Gmlistani, who grabbed him with one hand.' Before the edge came down arrother, Goer-kilt% sprang irt, and bayoneting ~him, pulled the trigger too, with a most charming grin. The `dead man's grasp dragged, Blundell down. Others saw that, and :thought hini killed; they raised a yell, and the Gnlistanis ran. • And as they ran the Goorkhas , -followed. There Ivere a hundred dead in that one ihot corner. ' Yet' this was but, the beginning, and when they looked ever the almost impossible cliff *they saw the- fight below. "Cope," said .33111adell, who was untouched, though the old wound on his shoulder was torn .open.. They ran along the path that the few flyi ; Gulistanis took and came out over and beyond the main fight. Perhaps it was well that some of the, tribesmen e,scaped, for when they ran down.and came inta the rear of their own force they brought a terrible ,alarm with. them. The BOYS ran forward to their fightins, lite, and when the remnant of Blundell's meeopened fire on them from the cliff , above their hearts failed them, they cried out, and wilted.; It was not 'Allah's decree that this should be a victrty. And now the Sikhs OA the far side of the river Were able to go over. The stone shoot bringing its ghastly burden of dead ceased to rattle and slide and with infinite care it was possible to cross it at the river's verge. Briggs shouted for joy ; the fight was over. ' "Keep them on the run." ,And when their few sappers managed to make _the stone shoot really possible, he ordered a general advance. 'He came across Blundell sitting on a rock half way down the defile. He was not a little exhausted. "Well dii4 Blundell," said the Colonel. But out 'of the hundred Men lie took up that hill only fifty were unwounded. And thirty were dead. "Sahib, are' you pleased with us or no pleased with us ? " said the Goorkhas, shyly, to Blundell. "Amid will you tell Gwynne Sahib you are pleased ? " , And when lie said he was pleased they prayed that Sri Gutman Gurak Nadi and Sri Ga,nga mother inSglit keep him very well. "Blundell Sahib is a great man," they cried. "With him and with Lef ten Gwynne 'when we meet the enemy so we cut them tip." That night they saw the silver Gul close at.liand, arid Major itaWSOll, pale and haggard, but cheerful. - with his arm in a sling, came 'Mit, and welcomed them. For after that last fight the Gulistanis raised ths siege, and the most desperate of them marched away to Jandol.

Cur APT E R XIII.' The campaign was practically over, and, wine was more, the quickness with which Briggs' fore, bad come over the KOralt, falling like a thunderbot on the Gulistanis, frightened the tribesmen from Gilgit to Quetta. It was his luck to drop, a It'imp ice on the bubbling pot of war, and new the ; headman of the villnes came in with many salaams and professed that Sekunder Azful had never beer. I Any friend ot theirs. Be' certainly was not beloved by them, ea now when he took to the north-west passes, and was mit likely to return; they remem- bered his misdeeds? and laid the death of many kinsmen at his door. The news went over all the frontier, 83 though it were flashed by the helio- graph, and was known in the bazaars of India and I even in Yarkand by the time it was heard in London I neross the Black Water. They told of Selomder Afzul's flight in Chitral and Bajoim; the Litm lan Kiwis sent it on to the Molinuouls; it was known ' over the Kamm River and the Safed Koh Ranges in Kurrunt and Kohat, by the.. time, that Begbie heard it in Swat. • Colonel •Briggs cousnlted with Rawson, and they sent Blundell in pursuit. of Sekunder. .thit he flew I li2ht.. and escaped by mountain paths. • i • "The arm of the Sirkar is very lonz," said the ' Hulistanis, "but Sekunder is a mountain goat. It was mit oar fault that we foaght against the Sirkar. We Must have been mad. Uo to, let us se:'• provisions. By the will of Allah it is now • , 27 But though Blniwiell did not catch the mountain goat he caught, or renewed, malaria, and was glad to get bark into CatllT) at Chili, where Storey ! quinmed him and ;witted him with fever -tindures, 1 and got him out again -by the time that Bri,gs was touch 4th the outpiims of the•Pe,hawur column. I Before that the heliograph was ;winking front the highest. hill (dose over the fort and the villagers shook their heads. "These Raab's understand black magic, and are. aPsiwedly lutist ‘vonderful devils," they cried. l's• With a looking-glass they Fpeak very far off. An army sits doom- mi,l says to the mountains ' Her I ant,' and another looking-glass says ; Ho, Ito! Is that you ? ' For that is the other tinny.' "You.stuff our livers with lies," said villagers, who had not beheld the winking wonder of the looking-glass. • "And what if there is a cloud and no sun ?" • • . .

"We Say tite truth, and it is as wonderful as their long-nosed animal in the Punjab," returned those who had seen it. "And if the sky be clouded, or it be night, be assured they have' some ether devilry to speak by. We have been told of talking lamps, and a long rope they !rhout through, 1 and a thin wire."

"God. is great !" cried the others. "And if it had been no more than a matter of tulwars we would assuredly have • cut them - up. But how can they . shout through a wire ? " i "Shaitan assists them," said the men of Gulistan. 1 "If it were not so how would these beardless boys, ! whom they call Goorkhas, those who chop off the :. headaof goats with their heavy little swbrds, have , beaten our best warriors?" - i "That is so," the strangers-agreed. "Tint who is ! their leader ? Is it the fierce one with white hair ! or the Black Devil?" "We are. of opinion it is the one, they call Blundell, the Black Devil, for he knows everything. i It was but yesterday one from Laru laid: '.Salaam, ! you infidel pig,' and be understood him, and said : something to one of these Goorkhas, who smote the man from Lam ti upon the nose so that the blood, gushed forth," said the Gulistanis. "But the one who was in the ,fort is the one who makes -11 l the arrangements. At least, so we are told. Brlt., see, they are even now speaking with the looking-g:ess I" ; And the next day Begbie's advance guard rode : into, the Gulistan main valley,: and a camp was picked for the whole force. 'Though the fighting appeared to be over; and, indeed, was over, a demonstration of the. real strength of the Indian ! /Government could do nothing but good. Too many of the tribesmen considered the .Sirkar able to do little more than snake an incursion and burn a Vfllage or blow, up a. tower. , In e t meantime Briggs brought down all the ? woun d who could yet move into Guli, and sent back he Guides over the Karak to those who were i at the small forts on the other side. .:For though the weather had herd up there was no necessity to return that way. Only those who were on the other 1 side of the main kotal would go back by Darband. . I I "Thank the Lord fOr that," said Billy, who did , not love snow. Sledging guns pleased him little. i "Mind you are not spoilt by your early taste of honour and glory; Gretton," Blundell told him. "Maybe it will be years till you have any more." i "Oh, I say," cried Billy, "what a horrible idea! You don't, think there'll be a beastly long quiet time .now, do you?" , . / For, seeing that Blundell understood the Gulistanis so well, he believed every word that fell 'from him. . 1

"Cheer up," field Blundell, grimly, "there will riever be peace on this frontier. After the boater is ours there is Afghanistan and then—Russia." Begbie was expected that afternoon, and every- thing. was ready for him. Colonel Briggs and Captain Rawson had ridden down the valley to meet him, but Blundell Was still on the sick list. From his tent, below: the signalling station he could see the flash of the distant. heliograph. Nothing very important was coining through Just then ; the pre- fixes to the messages were S.3L, or ordinary ones. "There's a private message coming through," . said Blundelt, lOoking through his glassei. "What, can you read it ?" asked Billy. • "I think everyone shonld be able to. I remember hearing that Lord Roberts can use the telegrph as well as most. operators. Suppose you,were :Milt up somewhere and your signallers were killed "Yes," said Billy. "But wlmt are they saying ?" "Get a pencil." - Billy took a pencil and a sheet of paper. "No, give me," said , ' —" said the' heliograph in its long and shorts. "It's to Rawson."
Blundell matle a few more remarks on his paper. ' "It's from his wife," he said, "and no business of caws. Hullo, what's that ? Another from London, and---"
" added the
heliograph. "It's to you Gretton." said 'Blundell. what? " cried Billy..

said the heliograph, rapidly. "Ah!" said Blundell. "It's from your sister:" . "By Jove What is it ? Oh what a wonderful chap you are to be sure," cried :hilly. • "Love to you all.--illadge." - Billy jumped up and laughed. "Oh, it's to you, too; Blundell. She'll be glad tmknow how well you did. Oh, won't she lust !" Ten minutes later .the messag,e was brought to Billy. - "I'll answor it at once " he utid, in pleased excitement. - • -

• "Send my love and best regards," cried Blundell, . "By Jove, now, I will," said Billy. So one. looking-glass spoke to the other, and the telegraph took it, and dot and dash went overland and under sea to the, dear under world of Englana. And next day they herd a review on the maidan where the *polo-ground was, and the extraordinary devils of Kaffirs did many wonderful things, and the,vainAikhs looked their best, and the deri:r little Goorkha devils their worst, and another fierce man with whiteish hair khanked them all round for their behaviour, and was especially gracious in an abrupt way to Rewsan and tio Captairi Mantua, who had ' been in/We fort with Rawson, and to Blundell and to Gwynne who watched the review from a dhooley. And what dear old Briggs had said about Gwynne and about Blundell in his despatchea and report was as good iis a V. C. for one and a iD.S.O.' for the other at. least; unless, of course, ,Fate stepped in, as it has a trick of doing. And the picnic which b,:gan at Darband and'Now- shera being now well Over, and the men of Gull having had a look al two animals with long noses, , beinginuch impressed thereby, there was a general° move towards the Pnnjab again, tot the men who I came up with Begbie were much disappointed at, I there being no fighting for them. The only glory got was the unostentations glory of the transport ' and commissariat. Though the food lacked haute cuisine of Ridiardson's horse, for once there was plenty of it. "My old man said 'e'ad to fight on a hempty belly, remarked one Tommy, "but so far's grub's concerned I ain't no badly complaint to make over his 'ere llow."
"And You'd grouse if you could, now Isiouldn't said his chum. "And why not, I'd like to know." answered the •flrst man. "'Oo d'ye take me _for ?"

And when they came to Mardan in their slow and dignified progress Briggs sent for Blundell iri the morning. The Colonel looked rather puzzled. "Captain Blundell," he said, "you are to ;o at once to Simla and report yourself to general Wills, the Del:nay-Adjutant-General." '"Yes, sir," said Blundell, ,who was obviously surprird. -

Atha the deuce could they 'wsnt with hi at headquarters ? Were they going to make more amends for their previous neglect ? It seemed hardly • likely,..fordn the A. G.'s departmen:: his name had never smelt sweet since old Dan !lad ruled the roost there. And yet he could believe anything now. "Before you go," said Briggs, with his hanti on Blundell's shoulder, "I want to tell you, Blundell, that I owe you a lot, and so does Rawson. For if it hadn't been for you we might have been a week later, and that week—well, you know What -it, means. And I think you deserve a ye, as nmch as 'Gwynne. But if you don't get proinotiom and D.S.O. it won't be my fault." . "'Thank you, sir, very much," said Blundell, with his heart. full. And you 'won't mind lily saying I'd sooner serve tinder you than any.inan know. -"I hope you will again," cried Briggs. you well enough yet to travel ?" Blundell smiled. "Ti) Simla ? Oh, yes; sir. I can stand ao much."

And the day after that he took tie train, and, staying a night in Lahore, on the fourth day was in Simla. Ile was still rather off colour, and his arm was not yet out/ of a sling, • hut he felt fairly tit for a man who has been wounded and had had malaria on top of it. Yet his nerve was a-little shaky. Confound it all, what: did the D.A.G. want with him ?

.lie sent in his name, and after ten minutes wait- ing was shorn itipt Genesal private room. Wills was a quiet, insignificant little man, with a memory like a rAlt-trap, and a real love of or4anisa- tion for its oweJ. sake. lie had been a Lginiental martinet, and now ruled his ()Mee wilt a rod of iron. But he desired to be just, and it-ever lost his temper. "Captain Blundoll !" "Yes, sir,". said BlundAl. ."I see you Were wounded in this affair," said the Generals "and I should like to itA you whether you are well enough to do yourself jnstice in any "natter ?" . • - -

div.head: WOMAN AND THE RACEHORSE.
div.p: WOMAN AND THE RACEHORSE.

I wonder how many women (except- the purely sporting ones) really enjoy the race meetings which -succeed one another with . such, bewildering rapidity during the season. writes Ella Hepworth Dixon. If they. were candid. not One in ten. For it is hopeless tor woman, -even at her loveliest, to compete , with the horse at his best. She must 'always feel her .inferiority in the eyes of the average Briton, and .it is, probably, with some sense of desperation that she makes such an extraordinary effort with her outward appearance at Ascot and Goodwood. She has to compete with the four-legged occupant e of the paddock, and is only too well aware that on these occasions 'of delirious excitement, -it is she who is the outsider. At cricket matches, re- gattas, and polo it is the samo thing in a minor degree, for the Englishman is usually preoccu- pied and serious chiefly when he is watching sports, and Sweet-and-Twenty will get small attention when the score is going up, or it .is a neck-and-neck race between two favourites. As the summer advances, large hats are once tigain resuming a high position in popular favour. A typical example of the up-to-clatts "grand chapeau is illustrated in our sketch. The straw of vrhich it is fashioned is a smooth, fine plait something similar tc) a Leghorn in style. but considerably wider. The hat has an immense brim, curving in graceful fashion over the face, and a. moderately high round crown.

Large roses. 'shading from a deep rich Crimson' to a delicate pink, wreath the crown completely. On the left sule is arranged An osprey' of green barley, matching in colour the green of 'the rose, foliage. This barley osprey, by the way, is quite one of the features of the new millinery, and has almost superseded the feather osprey. Similar affairs are made of all sorts of feathery grasses. • either in their natural colours or dyed to match the hat with which they are worn., QUEEN VICTORIA'S CONQUEST. • "

BY MORLEST ROBERTS,

CP...k.r.TER XII.

She 1133 Fvidm'Ly caught-, said Blundell, and he was greatly pleased., Thank Heaved he was doing well enough, and mig,lit have a chance to do better. If he really owed it all to her be Owed her some return, .Amt the notion was not unggeteful to him. His • imagination took fire, his face softened,, he -remembered her so well. She was very beattiful. He still,had that!'" little note to her in his pocket- book. • He took it out, and pencilled her name, on it in case of accident. _

There was every chance of one, assuredly ;.for if Gwynne ankhis Pathan,s and Goorkhas got up the cliff, they fould have to be supported, and the main attack must then be delivered by the way facing the big sangars. Blundell would lead that. Billy cursed the guns that time and wished he was in the(Goorkhas or the Guides. For his place was with the battery which would cover both advances.

When the night fell a4ain the Gulistanis were convinced that these Kaffir dogs of Englishmen, with their intlilol and renegade .men, were thoroughly: checked and beaten. Their Mollahs could not premise that the Kaffir bullets would turn into air on being fired Lthere were too matty dead for that, but they orouhsed them houris in Paradise quite up to the Prophet's speeification and far beyond any -sample they bga hitherto known on earth. And as they were of opinion, that the next thing would be a retreat on the part of the invaders they sharpened their tulwars again and anticipated much joy in cutting up stragglers. . "Most extraordinary devils these Kaffirs," said the Gulistanis. `"ls it true they have animals in the Punjab with tails at both ends ? " But instead of retreating • the ;Kaffirs opened a heavy tire on them an hour before dawn and made things so extieutely lint that it was difficult to go outside without at °ace taking a ticket for Paradise. And like most other pel-tple they were willing to defer that pleasure. A, few (nazis, cladjn white, were the only ones prepared for that journey in any Case. .

. . When the firing had lasted half an hbur Gwynn°, and his men, who had crossed the bed of the river at midnight, started on their climb. The din.was tremendous. It was still,dark and the night WBS heavy, overhead ; but fraiii all the cliff 'fire spurted incessantly. The guns were hot and jumped; the -nen serving them shouted, in spite of discipline, as the answering fire of the Gulistanis weakened and -died away: The day broke greyly, and Blundell, lying under ...k-slieltering rock, watched Gwynne and, his men, n hundred ante against the wall, that seemed- to overhung them and frown on their presumptuous effbrts. ' But still the enemy were unaware of the attack. When one moss daring than another she Wed his head he was shot down and dragged in by: the-legs. Only a few shots were returned. 4q,11e of these found 'their billet, and, thefgunners who were much \exposed, and firing at nriheard-of chise ranges,- sufl'ered badly. Billy-found nothing-to- complain of, forin half an hour he was in command of his battery. His senior Lieutenant joined Hunt in the hospital. The schoolboy of yesterday was the sole English- man with the. guns. Aud now he and the Colonel, who was 1)19147,11y in. shelter with the troops, _passed for the main -attack, could- see Gwynne within thirty yards -of the-top, just where the upper edge shelved, and a 'Clulistani looking (tarn might have seen theft too. The enemy_posted ligh- to the right on the far side of a big atone shoot saw the infidels.climb- ing, and yelled to the lower. beeastworks. The word ran like fire inflal,.•and leaped from ,sangar to sangar, till it reacted the one over Gwynne's head. They cared no more for ,shelter, but swarmed out, and stood hurling stones, and were shot down and replaced, and shot down and again replaced. :One of them fell with a lifted rock 7 in his hand. He collapsed, • screamed, and rolled• down headlong. Gwynne dodged the fallin,a.body, with-its clutching hands, and it struck a GOorkha and hurled 'him into mid-air. His-place was taken, and in a cataract of stones and is cloud of dust, the storm- • ing party rose inch by inch, and they laughed and yelled, and some fell back, and others trod on them, • and swung from point of rock to point. And overhead, a inollah yelled to Allah and ran. A Ghazi stood in hi a place, and, tulwar in hand, sprang, in the middle of the men. Gwynn, struck him with his fist, and a Goorklut beat hif brains out on a rock and, left him hanging. mv then those on the other ide saw Gwynne on lev4 ground, a Goorkha on one side, a Pathan ciit another. It was. quick work with the men, frovi , Napal. They fell over each other and tninbhE into the sangar, and the Gulistanis ran lihe rabbits, and were bayoneted and cut :down, ana many were crimped like cod. The heighf was won. And 'then, with the guns once more, thundering against the, „main 'line of sangars, • Blundell ft• the head .of the Main -body found himself slidina iaegdhaas ntd, down the broken path with his men after him, and 'how few were ,could not under: stand. tntihs y were rallied upon the level, and while Gwynne, non- bleeding a- three places, was at hand-to-hand work in the third sangar with his Pathans and Goorkhas mad wit. blood, Blundell was across the naafi ten yard; e ahead of his .first man, • and up the,opposing path. There the climbing qualities of the men told, they. zaught him up and would have passed him. H; grasped two of them. They turned to remonstrate, and the next ininute he was in front of them again. :And the, guns -ceased firing. e. There was one bloody ; moment of • it hand-to-hand, and 'then the -beaters Gulistanis ran. Blundell ft-mud himself shakin,, hands with Gwynne, and as he did so he wonderN what had hurt his arm. Blood ran,out of his sleeve and told him. • "A 'hot 'bit of work," he said; and till he grew' n little faint -he made them keep the enemy on ths run. - The path to the beleaguered fort appeared open, And not one of the officers was without a wound. The Colonel was hurt with a spent jezail an, to his great joy; Billy -found a finger missing. But Blundell's wound was no more than a cut in his - left deltoid. He Would take no rest on account of it, and when they found that their Colonel was only bruised (for lie did not know a rib was fractured till later) they pushed, on at once, rather recklessly, perhaps. But apparent reckless- ness is so often wisdom in dealing with such people that a dis Aster now and again hardly weighs down the greater advantages -of audacity. And consider- int, the slender -lines of communication, their forea weakened desperately by the necessity of leaving two of the junior officers at Karak and•Giddo in case of trouble" in it side valley, nothing could be more reckless now than caution. , "Hanged if I know whether, we're relieving Rawson or Rawson relieving us," said young Gwynne, who was in the highest spirits in spite of his injuries, as he Wasa;nre of being recommended for the V.(1., "for stay here we can't, and retreat would ho destaction. Happy times, when dtitY, desire, and necessity go hand in hand." ; "Sententious beggar," said the doctor, who was the only officer unwounded. :• : "It's philosophy," cried Gwynne. "I say, go easy." •

" ese your philGsophy now," said Storey, as he dressed his Ivounds. "'l've to use mine. I was in rreat hopes you'd all be badly hurt, and I'd have been in command. I'd much rather kill than mend."' "Yon can do balk". said Gwynne. • - Now only Blundell and Colonel Brit,gs and 13illv Gretton were able to move, and Blundell was ahead with the renuainirg Guides and Goorkhas. They pushed on ten miles and saw no more than a few tribesmen who loosed off their rifles and bolted. To-Morrow they promised themselves the near sight of Gulistan. That they were not now opposed chewed the Gnilistanis mnst, be still engaged with Rawson and his men. They left Storey with his hill hospital and a small guard at the nullah, and with three days' provisions went ahead all they Inew. - They camped that evening seven miles frim ttr.- end of the pass, and saw again the Gill River gleaming like a silver ribbon in green. Their advance guard was on the near side of a dangerous •:tone shoot neat the main camp. A mountain goat or sheep Could set the whole thing moving, and then the road was not to be passed without a lomg detour across the rocky river and back again. At early dawn, indeed before dawn, the advance bean, but when a quarter of the force was across the verge of the stone shoot there was sudden heavy fieinl. out of the hills above the defile. And in a moment the shipot was in movement, a tery avalanche was coming down; it was a great rock torrer.t. In the. grey light now breaking they saw s, big party of Gulistams on the hills engaged in keeping it going. "I'd better clear those out, Lir," said Blundell. And while Brion sent a detachment of Sikhs and

"To do inVself jti re.? " Blandon. " r beg your tirdo.ne• General Wills, but I hardly s understand." 'l'he General tapped his blotting-pad with a pencil. "We do not wish to be unfair to you," he said, sfter a moment's paise,. "but supposing you had a - :Awn brought. against you are you well enough to, beet6it at once ? ' . 'Blundell's imagination had thrown 6wers in his- path, but now an easterly wind blew. What could :ms mean F • "General Wills, if there is anything to be brought against me I am ready and anxious te hear it, and perfectly able to defend myself." The General nodded.
"You understand cipher well, I beliSVe. have ' been told you even invente% "Which was not adopted," said "And if so will you kindly sit down at this - desk," continued Wills.
Blunde,ll sat down and Wills pal a Itelegram in Front. of him.

_ "What-do you make of that, Captain Blundell ?" ' he asked, keeping his eyes on him. ' "It's a telegram partly in cipher and partly not,"' said Blundell, who was in great wonderment. "You cannot read it?" ' "With the ,key, of course, sir," said Blundell.. "But not without ?" Blundell looked up in-amazement: "I daresay it might be done in time," he said. 4 1 need not tell you that, sir." • Wills bored into him again with his eyes, ancr waited for a long minute till ho spoke. "This is a very serious matter, Captain Blundell, and I have been asked by the Commander-in-Chief to go into it as privately as possible. Do you give. Inc your word you do not know what this message means ?" "I give you my word of honour, sir," said Blundell. sternly,. "and I cannot understand wily it should be imagined that I do." "This is the key then," replied the ',entity Adjutant-General, and he handed, him a square card. "The word is—Rickshaw," said Blundell, and' taking a pen he began deciphering the wire, which read:
"Private. Chief, Simla. • Chief is desired by R AIR 1 M NHIVQ ALI 0 D N II to urgently request I W N RLT II 3.1. Q X•R CW N Cr A FY II I W be employed staff • Gulista:..— FIFLOING. ", •

The office of origin was Paris. "Is desired by the muttered Blundell, as he got it out, "that Captain BL-7N—(by ;love i)lie ,DE—LL—" stared at Wi11.., •• . . "'Why, that's me," he said, in •obvious surprise. it were not acted, thought Wills. "Go on, sir." "That Captain Blundell, 6th Punjab Cavalry, be .innloyed Staff. Guliatam " ire lay back in his chair. So Madge had got Sir .Dan to, do this, after till. And Yet--- He heard Wills tap on his desk again. • "This telegram, Captain. Blundell, is repudiated bir Sir paniel Fielding. It is a forgery!"

Motor Cyclists at Warrington. The reliability motor cycle trial promoted by the auto-cycle chilibas aroused consiberable interest in Warrington by reasdh of the fact that Warrington was the finishing point of Tuesday's run. The run com- menced on Monday when 59 motorists left Lands End on the journey to iohn a'Groat's, a distance of 889 , miles, To prevent *combing, it has been arranged to cover a distance of from 130 to 200 miles a day and any driver exceeding a maximum speed of 20 miles an hour is liable to disqualification. Tuesdays run was from Taunton to Warrington and the competitors were due to arrive here between 7.30 and ten o'clock. A large crowd asembled in -the vicinity of -Warrington bridge and, a hearty cheer greeted the first rider as he crossed the bridge, shortly after seven o'clock. The other drirrs followed in quick suceession, when a was founlj that the number of competitors had been reduced to 46. Miss Hind, the only lady driver, arrived shortly- before ten o'clock. The start from Warrington on 'Tuesday was made in a downpour of rain. The day's objective was Lockerbie (143 miles), and included the dreaded Shap Fell,and it was anticipated that the greasy and,difficult roads in Tuesday's run would cause havoc amongst the competitors. After leaving Warrington the ram cleared off, but the weather remained cold. The run to Kendal was made in good time, the first competitor arriving at 11.40, and twenty-seven others following within an hour. There was very little trouble on the toad, but' Miss Hind was stopped once oF twice for oil on the contract breaker.

div.head: LATE MR. SEDDON.
div.p: THE LATE MR. SEDDON.

St. Helens peaple heard with great regret of the death at sea on Sunday of Mr. Richard John Seddon, the Premier of New Zealand. Mr. Seddon was born on ithe 22nd of June, 1845, at Eccleston Hill. on the out- skirts of St. Helens, and was the son of Thomas Seddon, at different times grocer, poor-law officer, and school- master in the town. His mother was active among the 1 Primitive Methodists of St. Helens, and a tablet to her memory, set up by her son in MS, is to be seen in their local school.—At St. Helens on Monda,y the flags above the Town Hall and the Gamble Institute were floated at half-mast, while the Mayor cabled the following mes- sage to Irs. Seddon :—Profound sympathy from St. Helens.—Manrm, Mayor." St. Helens people have alWays taken great interest and pride in Mr., Seddon. 1"1is interest in the town was shown bv the fact that every Christmas numerous old reshlents received Christmas cards from him.
The Examiner, Saturday, June 16, 1906.
ST. JOHN AMBULANCE MAN --- Acknowledges First-aid Help Received from Lam-Buk.

Mr. Joseph Mellor, a St. John Ambulance Brigade expert connected with the Manchester Corps, acknow- ledges the purity and power of Zam-Buk, Nature's heal- ing balm and skin-cure. Mr. Mellor, who is employed on the Manchester City Tramways staff; and lives at 8, Dixon-street, Newton lleath,served six months with the forces in South Africa, and has had a very wide experi- ence in ambulance work. To a local reporter he said —" I have used Zam-buk for cuts, bruises, and sprains of every description,and have always found it excellent. An employee at the shed,who was suffering from inflam- mation of the knee, allowed me to dress it with Zam- Buk, as doctors' treatment was doing no good. The knee was in a shocking condition when I commenced I with Zam-Buk, but after three days there was a Very noticeable improvement. We used Zarn-Bak exclusively and the result quite reached our anticipations. The inflammation vanished under the cooling influence of Zam-Buk, and the knee became sound and healthy again. I have used Zam-Buk myself for an injured shoulder which gave me much pain, and here again the balm proved its worth by quickly banishing the pain and making the joint sound and strong. In all my experi- ence I have coma across nothing that acts so conSist- ently and so surely as Zam-Buk." Zam.Buk is being officially adopted by experts in skin-troubles and first-aid throughout the country. It should be kept handy everywhere.

div.head: PROSPEROUS BUILDING SOCIETY.
div.p: A PROSPEROUS BUILDING SOCIETY.
Annual Meeting at Warrington.

Another properous year's working has just been com- pleted by the Warrington Workingmen's Permanent Benefit Building Society. Details were 4ubmitted at the annual meeting of members of the society which was held in Golborne-street schoolroom on 'Monday evening ander the presidency of Mr. J. W. /touchier. There was a good ettendance which included the secretary (Mr. Peter Dalton). The CHAIRMAN said they had the same kind of balance sheet to offer the meeting as they had during the past few yeamand he thought they would be able to declare the same dividend. They would all agree that it was so far satisfactory. Daring the year the total income had been 24,039 and the cost of d,oing that business was £73 4s. There were only two ways of pro- ducing a dividend', and they were by making plenty of profit or keeping down the expenditure. They could not make a very big sum because they were limited in their operations, so the next thing was to keep down the expenses. In that respect no one could grumble at I lan outlay of £73 in doing a business of over £4,000. 1 There was a fresh t paragraph in the report and it was the result of a question which was asked at. the last annual meeting, namely, how much was owing, on mortgage to the society. The Secretary had dealt with the matter, and it would be seen that the total amount was £10,853 is., an& the valuation of the pro- perty upon which the advances had been mAe was £19,924, almost double, so that they might consider they had ample margin upon all the money which had ' been lent. (Hear, hear). They had not been troubled very much on the withdrawal side,and their membership was only seven less. The income kept steady, and all they wanted now was to find some good property upon which to lend a considerable amount of money that was' doing no good in the bank. (Hear, hear, and applause).

THE REPORT. The thirty-sixth annual report was submitted as follows :—During the year the sum of £1,679 13s. 4d. has been received as subscriptions ; £2,354 4s. for repayments; and £5 Bs. 3d. entrance fees, S:c., making the total receipts £4,039 ss. 9d.; the working expenses being £73 4s. The withdrawals amount to £1,369 Os. 11d. The sum of £2,250 has been advanced to members. There am t 209 subscribers, holding 2781 shares; and 40 borrowers, holding 2071 shares; making 249 members, bolding 486 shares. The bonuses this year amount to £393 13s, on the amount lent, of which sum £72 Os. H. is divided as profit, and £321 15s. carried to the Prospective Interest Account. Under the Build- ing Societies' Act, 1894, the accounts of all Building Sofdeties are required to be made up in such a form, and to contain such particulars as the Chief Registrar of Friendly Societies may, with the approval of the Secre- tary of State, direct. The form of account which has been prescribed by the Chief Registrar requires that the balance of capital remaining due upon the mortgage securities should be stated separately from the prospec- tive interest thereon; in other words the balance of the £B2 10s. (the nett amount advanced per £100) remaining unpaid to be distinguished from the balance of the £l7 10s. (the bonus charged) also remaining unpaid. The accounts of the Society for the past year have been made up on this basis,and work outas follows : The total amount remaining owing upon mortgages is £10,853 Is., of which only £9,361 17s. can be regarded as capital, the balance of £1,291 4s. representing the proportionate amount of interest thereon, calculated for the number of years the several mortgages have still to run. The profits for the year, including £l5 9s. 11d. from last account, after deducting working expenses. amount to £374 145., out of which the Managers recom- mend a dividend of 4 per Gent, which will take £356 18s. Id., leaving a balance of .Cl 7 13s. lid, which they direct to be carried forward to next year's account. The total amount owing to the society on mortgages is £10,833 Is. The valuation of the property upon which the advances have been made is £19,923. The whole of the Managers retire. Messrs. Harding, E. Wallington, Isherwood, Bouchier, W. H. Wallington, and Baxter are eligible, and offer themselves for re-elec- tion. Six additional managers will be taken from the ' register in rotation. The CHAIRMAN pointed out that there would be £450 in the bank after providing for the interest to be paid the following Monday. Mr. E. WALLINGTON moved the adoption of the e dTaocemoatinnyt obfu tt bheems,unpopodsoeudbitt, reportt seemed and da bavl ea rnyc e isnhveoeltv. was all owing to the frnudnlent secretaries who had held office in some building societies in times gone by that these precautionary measures had been forced upon them by Act of Parliament. He thought that when such a statement as they had heard was properly audited and sent up to the Registrar General it was I almost an impossibility for a secretary to defraud. He commended the Society most heartily to all the mem- bers, as it supplied a very easy means of obtaining property. It was also a compulsory way of saving. By depositing a little more with the Society than they paid in rents to a landlord, in nine and a half years the property become their own. Mr. E. ENGLAND seconded and congratulated the managers on the position of the society after thirty-six years working. He thought, however, that the people of Warrington were not taking the advantage of the benefits of the society that they ought to do, and every effort should be made to bring those benefits promi- nently before the public. The report was adopted. THE DIVIDEND.
On tbe motion of Mr. GREALY, seconded by Mr. Clumcocx, it was decided to pay a dividend of -1 per cent.
The CHAIRMAN said the stability of the Society was such that if it had to be wound up the members would receive 20s, in the £ and interest on their money right up to the winding-up.

ELECTIONS. The retiring managers were re-elected, so that the Board of managers is now constituted as follows : Jamea Harding (Chairman),E. Wallingtou,Robert Isher- wood, J. W. Bouchier, J. Baxter, W. H. Wallington, Gilbert Ford, E. England. J. Harding, jun., E. Hesketh. J. Grealy, and William Gregson, Messrs. William Bodle sun., and Robert Lee were ro-elected surveyors, and Messrs. A. W. Howard and George Armstrong , surveyors.
The usual grant of Is. per meeting for each manager was sanctioned.
A vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman an the proposition of Mr. Isherwood seconded by Mr. Gregso_nt _ .

Special reference was made to tlie admirable work of the secretary who it was pointed out, had for some years only been absent from one meeting of managers each year. The chairman remarked that Mr. Dalton did his work exceedingly well for the money he received.

div.head: [ALE RIGHTS RESERVED. FOR THE DEFENCE.
div.p: [ALE RIGHTS RESERVED. FOR THE DEFENCE.
! Br BEATRICE ATHELSTAY, Author of "A Sprig of Mistletoe," "The Sergeant's. Story," "The Girl From the West," "Hetty's. Suitors," "Sunshine and Mist," tte.

The train was just allout to leave Manchester Exchange, and Bertram Keen, the well-known barrister,, gave a sigh of relief at finding himself alone in a first-class carriage. Drawing a number of papers from the bag he carried, he scattered them broadcast over the seat,, and then brought Out his cigar-case and prepared to think, for he was on his way to a difficult case in the country, and his brief needed: yet some studying. His life was so busy that railway journeys could not be thrown in as times of recreation; he was apt to relegate some of his chief mental work to them.'

On this occasion, however,, his privacy was to' be disturbed, for at the last moment the guard ushered in a breathless woman, who nearly fell over Bertram's long legs, which he had disposed -if in such a manner as to monopolise most of the compartment. He apologised, albeit with some- thing like a scowl. The new-corner, confused and distressed, apologised also, tliough she was not in. fault Then the train started, and Bertram ,collected his papers into a neat little bundle and ' looked out of the window, unreasonably annoyed. He felt this woman's presence as an intrusion. _ He wanted to think—he wanted to smoke, and it i was not a smoking-carriage. He was feeling too ill-tempered to ask his companion's permission, and she, though she witnessed the transference of I the cigar-ease from the seat to his pocket, ' ! dared not to make a suggestion, for she was intuitively conscious of his vexation. Bertram Keen was not an unamiable man; on ' the contrary, he was kind, just, and generous. j But there are times when the unwonted presence of another grates on the nerves, and appears as an affront This was one of them._

Marion Lee, feeling like a scolded child—or rather like tile dog, whose characteristic it is to take unmerited chastisement with a feeling of humiliation untinged by resentment—watched him furtively. He had a keen, clever face— elean-shaven, with the Hibernian contrast ot ,blue eyes and black hair. The nose was curiously tip-tilted, and, together with the large, scornfully curving lips, suggested a kind of sneering insolence, as if a scathing remark would fall naturally from him. But this impression was contradicted by the boyish candour of the upper part of the face; the eyes and brow were irresistibly winning. , For a long time Bertram Keen nursed his imaginary grievance, knowing well that he would laugh at himself for it a few hours later. When the train stopped, the woman in the further corner, on whom he had not bestowed a second glance, rose to depart. All at once he relented, and wished lie-Thad been more polite. He hastened to open the door for her.

"Your journey ends here? he asked. "I want to find another carriage," she said, timidly. "What a brute 1 have been!" Bertram ejacu- lated fiercely to himself. Aloud he, said: 'Let me go and look for a place for yout I fear the train is very full; people are rushing to the seaside this mouth. Pray de not come out, the platform is crowded." , He swung himself out, and Marion saw his tall hat moving about amongst ,the throng of people. He went from one end of the train to the other, and then returned to her, wearing a totally digerent face from the one which had scowled upon her so .forbiddingly. It was lit up by a pleasant smile, full of friendliness, and her heart warmed instinctively at the sight of him. "It's no use, I'm afraid," he said. , "Every place is occupied. I'm sorry, if you wanted particularly to change." "I have a third-class ticket, that is all," she murmured, telling haif the truth. She looked like a third-class passenger. "Oh, that doesn't matter at this season. I take a first myself, because I usually have some work to do;and I like to be undisturbed—but you do not disturb me," and he laughed with a pleading glance of apology. "I hope not," she said, greatly relieved, and subsiding into her corner again. 'Pray smoke if you wish to—and forget me. I will read the newspaper." She took up one which had been left in the carriage. Restored to a good temper which was only disturbed by self-reproach, Bertram Keen returned to his brief, but not before he had taken ; a survey of his companion. When she had spoken to him, the effort calling up a faint flush in her delicate cheeks, she had seemed quite a girl—not, as he had thought at first, a mature woman. Now it was slifficult to decide the point of her age. She had a pale. Madonna-like face, the difference between it and that of the conventional Madonna lying in the square, determined chin and long; straight line of the mouth. She was very beautiful, but so quiet in her demeanour that it needed a second ; glance to discover the fact. Bertram did not quite know whether his mother would consider: her a lady. She might be a governess, or some- thing of that sort. Meanwhile the scenery through which they ; were passing had become very picturesque in character. They were nearing the sea, and in; the land of gorse and heather. Red hills, blushing gloriously from base to crown, rose On every side, and the hardy Welsh mountain sheep ' bounded from rock to rock with an agility un- known to their brethren in the lowland pastures. Presently a whiff of sea-air came through the open windows, and the train began to sway from side to side in a provincial manner. Flocks of sea-gulls passed gracefully over the stretches of sand in one of the most beautiful estuaries in the world, and the sight of a Lancashire cotton- spinner armed with a gun, taking reckless aim at them as they flew by, brought to mind Heber's fiescription of a land no fairer, surely, than this, "Where every prospect pleases, And only man is vile."

Bertram Keen pocketed his papers with a long sigh—this time of satisfaction, for he saw his way clear before him—and gave himself up to the enjoyment of nature for the few minutes left to him. He had forgotten Marion Lee. She, top, was unconscious o his presence, for as she drew near the journey's end, an expression of anxiety which had settled on her features as soon as Bertram's rudeness had ceased to trouble her, deepened, and she sat gazing into vacancy with her hands clasped tightly before her. On alight- ing, Bertram lost sight of her, for the case which he was defending began at half-past ten, and already the hands of the big church clock were pointing to the half-hour. _ .

Wiila a few hasty strides he left the station behind him, and in an incredibly short space of time was seated at the counsel's table facing a row of solemn country gentlemen and local shop- keepers who seemed thoroughly to enjoy their position as magistrates, and witi his back to a surging crowd; for the case was one which had attracted wide attention in circles the very exist- ence of which was a kind of myth to most of the residents in this sheltered Corner of Britain. It was the "visitors "—that yearly godsend to the little town—who filled the police-court with unaccustomed colour and with a rustle and a murmur only kept in check by the constant "Silence!" uttered in stentorian .tones• by a stalwart policeman, who seemed to enjoy his position even more than the magistrates did theirs. The incurious townspeople, who knew i Mrs. L'Estrange as a neighbouring landed pro- prietor merely, had not come to hoar her case— one of the most cruel, her counsel honestly con- sidered, ever brought before a British bench. Bertram Keen• strove as a rule to keep himself free from personal interest in the affairs of his clients, but a visit to Mrs. L'Estrange had affected him against his will, and as he now glanced along the row of mediocre faces on the • bench before him, a smile of passionate contempt and irony gave his strong lips a more men- tuated curl than usnal.. For he recoguised that net one of these men. set there to judge a _woman Who had devoted' a long life to works of philanthropy, had suflici:3nt intelligence to appre- ciate eithcrher intellect or the wide horizon of her charity. It was the constant contemplation of such benches that had given that expression of habitual scorn to a face which otherwise had persisted in its boyishness long after his early manhood was nest. Mrs. L'Estrauge, after a very unhappy married life which had culniii tted in a separation, had become celebrated as s champion of women, and had undertaken the difficult and often dis-

heartening. work known,ffs "rescue." Her institu- tions and her methods were famous, and like all reformers, she had made both friends and foes. A chance of injuring her had presented itself to the latter, with the result that Bertram Keen had been engaged to defend her character against the blackest stain—that of ill-treating and morally injuring one of the objects of her tenderest and most anxious dare. The young barrister sat and listened to the counsel for, the prosecution, his quick mind taking note of every point in the speech which he afterwards meant to dissect cruelly. How easy it would be to him to demolish that structure of lies! He had no doubt at all of convincing the public—all those eager listeners at the back. But What if, as he had reason to fear, this were a packed bench? In that case it would be a tight to the death! He must make them feel ashamed of themselves, these little- minded nonentities usurping the seat of Solomon! He would make them writhe—force them as Balaam was forced, to utter what they had not willed. His face looked almost cruel as he made this resolve. "Pshaw ! The fellow grows wearisome," said Bertram tollimself, stretching his long legs as far as he dared under the table and tilting his chin' at his adversary. Seeing that this had some effect, and that the other lost a period, he slowly moved himself round in his chair and took a cool survey of the back of the court. Suddenly his heart seemed to cease beating. He had just caneht sight of, Marion Lee, and her image hal seized upon hinlt with that strange grip that sometimes comes unexpectedly to shake the foundations of a strong''nature which had thought itself secure against attack. An intuition mounted turbulently, like wine, to his head—the knowledge that he loved. Never before had a face produced that effect upon him! It was not the result of thought, of criticism and admiration. It was something which came to him from outside, against his will; a voice that said plainly, unmistakably in his ear, refusing to be silenced, "This woman is yours." Marion did not see him. Her eyes were fixed on one point —the back of the head of the young solicitor who was stating the case for the prosecution. Her lips were half parted, her face white as death. Bertram

With a supreme effort o, returned to the intricacies of the case, and when the time came for the cross-examination of witnesses he was as collected as ever, and carried away the audience, as usual, by the searching nature of his questions and the rapidity and brilliance of his repartee. One after another the witnesses retired dis- comfited, and Bertram k,eenly enjoyed his triumph—the more so, as he knew that Marion's eyes were fixed upon him with the same rapt attention as they had been on his adversary, but, he hoped, with a friendlier interest. The case was of a wearisome length, and the heat in the crowded court grew more and more oppressive. Bertram created a certain sensation by referring in his speech to the state in which he had found his client She was suffering from an illness which for many years had been con- cealed; who could tell how far its rapid develop- ment was due to the anxiety occasioned her by a cruel accusation? At last the solemn magistrates filed out. It was a moment of intense strain, perhaps, to many—certainly to Marion Lee. Bertram Keen knew it, and he resolved to send her encouragement in a glance. Rising to his full height he bent his searching gaze upon her and succeeded in conveying to her what he 'wanted to say. She blushed, trembled a little, and gave a grateful half-smile in recognition of her late travelling companion. The magistrates returned as Bertram resumed hisiseat. He leant back in his chair and began tapping the table with his fingers. For the first time in his life he felt nervous about a verdict— neryous for the sake of the woman he loved, whose anxiety had communicated itself to him. At this moment a telegram was put into his hands. He read it, and his face blanched. The chairman had risen and was about to pronounce the verdict. He must be stopped! At all hazards he must be prevented from uttering words which might be not only cruel, but sacrilegious. Bertram sprang to his feet. "Your w rship--" The chairman suddenly collapsed into his eliair, overcome by the audacity of counsel, but entirely dominated by a will-power superior to his own.
t will

"Si--lence" began the stalwart police- man, but the word withered on his lips. "Gentlemen," said Bertram, in a tone of piercing sadness, "defer your judgment on the actions of the dead. Mrs. L'Estrange passed away suddenly at her residence less than half- an-hour ago." , A great murmur arose in court. The policeman dared not repeat his mechanical cry, for Bertram's eye' unwittingly resting upon him, seemed to fix him in a vice. Suddenly one word was uttered in a tone of anguish which thrilled every;eoul present. "Murdered ! " -

Th—e-a.of a heavy fall followed. In moments of supreme excitement men are not always careful of the choice of their words. It was an oath which rose to Bertram's lips as he flung himself over the few benches which lay between himself and Marion Leo, pushing aside their occupantsmmith brutal determination. His ,brain was in ft turmoil of fury against those who had, to gratify a petty personal malice, brought about this tragedy. Sonic of them were present, and his hand fell none the less heavily oh their shoulders when they obstructed his, path. In a few seconds he was beside the fainting woman. He helped ta carry her to a neighbouring shop, where a kind-hearted lady waited upon her. A doctor who happened to have been in court followed. ' Bertram waited, 'sitting in the little parlour. It was long ere she recovered, and then the doctor declared that she was hardly fit to travel. She was in an extremely w •ak .condition, and seemed as if she had been insufficiently nourished, and overworked. The lady who had interested herself in her was anxious to keep her for the night, but the patient shrank from attention, and insisted on returning to Manchester by the earliest train possible. _

Bertram undertook to see her safely home,- and so theso two made the return journey together. What a difference those few hours had made! She was too weak and weary, and too overcome with grief, to object to the young barrister's attentions, and she allowed him to take her to her lodgings in a dreary street, where the land. lady informed him that she was a typist, working for a livelihood all day, and doing deeds of charity at night. "Not but what she's quite respectable herself," said the woman. "And a more regular payer I never knew, nor a quieter party. But they do say she goes to them rescue homes and talks to the women. She has her own latchkey, and I asks no questions." So this was the life she led!

What was it that had bound her 'with so strong a tie to the woman who had died that day? The one of patrician descent, and with great wealth nobly dispensed. The other, poor, unknown, a toiler for her bred in a great city! Bertram's heart contracted with a sudden pain as be recalled a sentence she had uttered that afternoon. It was her sole reference to the dead. "I owe everything to her—everything; honour, life itself. She saved me from an awful fate." He had not realised it at the time; now ho thought he knew; He saw his fair Madonna— s repentant Magdalene, trying to wash out the past by holding out a hand of rescue to her sisters.
_ A poor, sad little unit in the city! A wrecked life, and 1. present of sordid conditions
But ho hived her.

"Bertram, you .will ,)ever know what your mother has sacrificed to you. You are brealing my heart, boy." ."Mother, wait and see her before you judge. She is a woman to grace any man's home." "She has never confessed to you." , • "She has told me all I want to know." Mrs. Keen sighed deeply. She was a stately lady, who suited well the massive furniture and handsome draperies of the old town house in which she dwelt with her son, the pride of her life. This was the bitterest momept she had ever known, but she shewed no wea-kness. She was Waiting to receive Bertram's promised bride, who was coming to dinner that evening. Marion had insisted that she Would not be fetched, and .I.;eltrain was therefore sharing Ins motuer-s suspense, expecting her. • Ile had spent many hours with her since their' first meeting, and his love had grown steadily with the knowledge of her eharneter. She was , indeed his ideal woman, and if she had a past, , he only blessed that past because it had made, her what She was.

The papers had been full of Mrs. L'Estrange's death; and the dramatic incident of the unknown woman who travelled from Manchester to attend the case, and who had fainted in court, had been freely commented on. She was spoken of as "one of the thousands, doubtless, to whom the deceased lady had been a saviour and a benefactress."
"I deserve it," was Marion's , comment, when Bertram had brought the insult to her notice. He had hoped that she would pronounce it a libel. He bore the blow bravely, and loved her the more.
Every day ne brought her home from the office where she was employed, but she resisted inquiries as to how she spent her evenings, and he forehore to make them.

_ Once or twice she had startled him by the announcement that she was going away the next day, And he had accidentally discovered that she went to London. But of these journeys she gave no account. His trust was absolute.

A cab drew up -to-iie.Cl-c-m--r-,-;.Q-lertram, his impatience grown too great, for formalities, hastened downstairs and met In the hall a lady whom at the first glance he took for a stranger. It was Marion, dressed as he had never seen her before, and looking startlingly handsome. She was, as usual, entirely in black, but the material eas velvet, and she wore a string of large pearls round her neck.

She laid her hand lightly on his arm, and her eyes shone with suppressed excitement as she said simply: "Take me to your mother, Bertram. ' Trs. Keen was overcome with astonishment and admiration ,to the point of being nervous. The dinner passed off well, however, chiefly owing to the tact and charm of the visitor. When the mother's heart was fairly won, and they sat in the drawing-room over a log-fire, talking of the future openly and with a serious happiness, Marion laid her hand on Bertram's and said, quietly: "There isl,a confession which I owe to you both."

Mrs. Keen shuddered, and tried to ejaculate. "No, don't, dear ! " But Bertram said, unfalteringly: "What you wish to say I shall love to hear." "I believe you are the noblest man on the earth !" she cried, with sudden passion. "I have let you live under a cruel misapprehension, but it came about in the first place so unavoid- ably, and though I could have cleared myself to you, there would have been thousands still believing the lie and—l did not see why you should be the exception. What did it matter? I asked myself. But it did matter, and I was deceiving myself. I wanted to try you, to see whether you could be as magnanimous as a woman is usually expected to be. Now I will tell you why I went to hear that cruel case— why I fainted when you made that announce- ment. Mts. L'Estrange was my mother." "Your mother!" Bertram began dimly to recall that he had heard of Mrs. L'Estrange having a daughter, who was absent at the time of her death. Since then he had thought no more about the matter.

"Yes, I am Marion L'Estrenge—my mother's heiress, and I am going to carry on her work. My lawyers know all my history, and why I wanted to keep quiet these few months. People think lam abroad. I told you once that my mother had saved me from an awful fate; it is true. Her influence did it. All through my childhood I was a disputed possession. My mother wanted me' to bring me up according to her own ideas. My father, whom I adored, wanted to make a toy of me. I loved him best, until I learnt to know him. At last I was given the choice with whom I would live. My mother warned me, with tears of anguish. I refused to believe her story. I considered that she had sacrificed her wifely duties to her philanthropy. I, a child, who knew nothing of the world, judged her. I,said those cruel words to my pother, whose wrongs I now know to have been unendurable! So we parted in bitter- ness. I lived with my father in the Riviera, or in Paris—anywhere where there was excitement, and what I then called pleasure. I cannot relate how my eyes were opened—it is too horrible a story. I will only say that he cast me off—my fortune was dissipated, and I was penniless. He died soon after. My mother thought that he could not touch my money—she never knew that part of the story; and thinking I had gone my own way, she counted me lost to her. But I returned to England, and tried to earn a living by teaching. That failing, I took to type- writing, which I had once had a fancy to learn, and so I came to settle in Manchester. My object was to prove myself worthy of my mother before falling repentant at her feet. I did not know she was ill, and thought the future was mine. I became a voluntary helper at the "Refuge," where lam well known. They call me Sister Lee. Some day i bad hoped to take my mother a record of the work of Sister Lee, and lay it before her as an offering of atonement. It was my mistake. I should have gone to her empty-handed, for she would have forgiven me freely. I have learnt, Bertram, that there is such a thing as free forgiveness and pure-hearted magnanimity in the world. But my mot4ser, alas! will never know."

Mrs. Keen, weeping surreptitiously, murmured something about "faith" and "a mother's blessing." But Bertram, condensing into one look such ineffable scorn and satire that it seemed as thobgh he would have no further store to draw upon for professional purposes, and hiding his faee in his hands because he could bestow that look oil no one but himself, declared: "I've been the biggest fool lately that evei have had to deal with ! " rTHE END. 1

if its terms are not more strictly defined when it again comes up for discussion on th( Report stage of the Education Bill. It was the consequence of an amendment moved from the Liberal side of the House by Major SEELY. The proposal was that where a Voluntary school is not taken over by the local authority the owners or trustees may appear before the Board of Educa- tion, which shall hold a local inquiry, and if in the opinion of the Board the local education authority has, without good and suffi- cient reason, failed to make any proposal or arrangements for carrying on such a school as a provided school, they may be required to take such a school upon such terms as the Board may determine, The amendment was strongly sip- ported by Mr. DinoN, who has been a great con- ciliatory force during the debates on the Bill. Mr, DILLON'S point was that the local authorities under the Bill as it stands might say, " We will get rid of Voluntary schools and build new schools." That, he said, was not the avowed intention of the Government, and was no part of the programme with which the Liberal party went to the electors of the country. If the Government were going to pass a Bill to destroy the Voluntary schools of the country and drive the children elsewhere, Mr. Diuoli begged it to say so. Mr. DIRRELL exhibited his usual sympathetic feeling for those who really believe, as Mr. DILLON does, that the Bill as it stands might create cases of great hardship. Ho was willing, he said, to introduce at a later stage of the Bill a proposal which will place both parties in a fair and equal position. The arrangement made must, however, be of a reciprocal character. The owners or trustees might have a right to appeal to the Education Board where the local authority refuses to take over a school that is offered to it, but, on the other hand, the local authority must have a right of appeal when a school is withheld which it desires to acquire.

This seems a good working arrangement, but it requires to be carefully safeguarded. In actual practice it will probably mean that the nation will be saddled with a great many schools which wit be only partially fit far the purpose they are designed to serve, for the tendency always is in such cases to make the community pay more than full value for what it acquires. Many old schools will be made to serve where a corresponding num- ber of new schools ought to be built. But there is anotherand more important consideration. There may be denominational schools of excellent quality where they are really not needed—where, in fact, they are wholly superfluous, so far as any ; scheme .1 national education is concerned. They may have been built in rivalry to Board schools where no additional school was needed. Unless Mr. BIRRELL carefully hems round his new provision with safe- guards these schools are kalmost certain to be forced on the local education authorities. The natural and just arrangement will be a provision that no school shall be taken over by the local authority unless it is a necessary part of the • educational equipment of the locality in which it exists. The difficulty which is thus, raised has its entertaining side. When the Educa- tion Bill was first introduced there was a general cry of " confiscation " from the denomina- tionalists, on the ground that the local authorities were to have power to acquire the schools hitherto called Voluntary. The Bishops and their friends have thought matters over more carefully since then, and they are now falling over each other's
