The " Observer" still CHINESE LABOUR. appear 4 to think it has a good case with regard to Chinese Labour against the Liberal Government in general and ourselves in particular. We do not, which, is perhaps, quite natural. Our contemporary continues to harp on the fact that 16,000 coolies had been imported since the present Government took office, notwithstanding that Chinese Labour was "denounced as slavery by the Liberals. What the " Observer" omits to tte is of course considerably more essential to a de understanding of the case than the state- !lents which are emphasised. Like Mr. Robert I -rierpoint in a recent speech,the Tory organ holds 11l) these 16,000 new arrivals as a horrible example of Radical perfidy while shanathilly ignoring the all-important fact that the licenses for these coolies' were issued by the late Government in the closing days of its rule. It is true—as we frankly admit than the new Government might have cancelled these licenses and paid the necessary cmnpensa- ton. Possibly also, they were in some degree rnorally bound to do so by the tenour of the °Neches during the election campaign. But who lv.ould have been the first to scream out maledic- tion if such an unconstitutional course had been taken ? Why, the" yellow" journals and Tory Press generally! We should soon have been lilformed in glowing terms how much of the tax- Payers' money was being thrown away to satisfy paa "Nonconformist conscience "or some equiva- nt thereto. No, this outcry—for party purposes --against the Government on the Chinese Labour clilestion does not ring true. It is spurious coin, !!!ad we think the elector possesses enough know - 'dge of the question to realise that the Govern- it has done its best to cope with difficulties Itionally created by its predecessors in office.l

is a phrasve which has a very real meaning—not, perhaps, strictly that which it was intended to convey. A popular King's Counsel, lately deceased, tells, in hie reminiscences, of a well-educated friend of his Who imagined that every barrister to whom it was given to place the letters " K..C." after his name 6ejoyed a comfortable allowance of £3,000 per I:lnum from the State And of the customs and ibits of the Inns of Court there is equal ignor- ice among people who by birth and education lit be presumed to know better. Perhaps 44e greatest of all mysteries to the man the street is how the barristers manage ~c) make a living. If he glances at the Law List" be will find there an array of l'oreething like 20.000 barristers. England is not a Particularly litigious country—not so much 80 444 Ireland, for instance—but even were the ten- keney to go to law twice as great as it is it would "a difficult to find constant employment for this reat army of lawyers. Of course, as a matter of act, a comparatively small proportion of them are ..12'ractising barristers—a fair estimate says about t'o. Y 00Man of the others have never intended practise, having sought the distinction merely ic't status. Others have been forced by inability r° get briefs into authorship or journalisim. The eal work of the Bar is in the hands of the few.

1; , The late Alderman John THE Lira Roberts was one of our most ALDERMAN devoted local public men ROBERTS. and we fe9l sure we are expressing the sentiments of all who knew him when we say that his death will be sincerely regretted by all parties and ranks of the community. He had done good service to the town in more than one capacity but we venture to say that his most enduring memorial lies in his untiring labours on behalf of a noble institu- tion—the Infirmary, lie took a fatherly interest in the Workingmen's Committee, stimulating the exertion of the members with , words of praise and good cheer, and to no- 1 one was it a sonrce of greater pride to see the steady advance in the workingmen's contrib- butions. It is a touching recollection that his last public appearance in the town which he loved SO much was to support the claims to the gener- osity of the towns people of the Infirmary and District Nursing Association on the occasion of the Horse Parade. Though politically he was an nuYeilding Conservative and a sturdy fighter, he na always most courteous towardS his opponents Was whom he had many close friends. He a hard-working Councillor and he never isgilised the satisfaction which his recent election to an aldermanic seat afforded him. His speeches Were perhaps not polished and his sentences were not couched in flowery language, but one felt instinctively that he was expressing his con- scientious convictions and he was never happier than when commending some worthy cause to the support of his fellow-townsmen. TRADE UNION approval of the Council's GROWL, conduct in undertaking the painting of the markets by direct labour recruited from the ranks of the Unemployed is marred by one discordant note, and that comes, strangely enough, from the Trades Council. It was at the instigation of Councillor • Stott, the secretary of that body, that the unusual course referred to was adopted in the painting of the markets. In a way, Councillor Stott, as repre- senting Labour, gained quite a notable triumph. Moreover the job has been well and economically done, and has found work for upwards of 60 men who would otherwise have been earning practically nothing. We should naturally have expected that the Trades Council would have been particu- larly pleased at the success of the experiment. tut no, another and decidedly selfish question has Cropped up. The men employed were not aU trade unionists—though "a man's a man for a' that "—and are Trades Council now regrets that ,", only Trade Union labour " was not employed on "le work. Some of the members spoke on Tuesday with a bitterness which proves what scant concern they really have for the rights of labour. They— the representatives of the workers—would create a Monopoly of their own, while condemning savagely Monopoly everywhere else. We have not come a 059 anything so mean and paltry for a long sxe. Why should only trade unionists be Ye -Pio d Are there no honest, capable, and th • rlfty workers outside the trade unions? If the -(own Council were to say, in such a case as this, that none but trade unionists need apply, they degerve to have the windows of their 4' Chamber smashed by the unemployed. We have a this deal of adtniration for the trade unions of 'uis country, but when members betray such a Illean and selfish spirit as was in evidence at the Trades Council on Tuesday, they bring their cause into disrepute and themselves under the contempt of all true democrats. div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

" The Bawl.' " refers quite coolly to " our quaint winding streets." This is the unkindest cut of all. And with Bridge-street before us too ! Good servants are becoming so difficult to obtain that we really cannot blame the American lady who disinherited her son because , he married her maid.— "Punch." . .

* * The latest sensation from Cronton, reported by a contemporary, is connected with coal boring and is to the effect that "the borehole, which has a diameter of from seven to eight inches, has arrived at a consider- able depth." , *t • * The employees of Messrs. !Crosfield are to be con- gratulated on securing such a splendidly-appointed recreation ground as the one which will be opened in Hood-lane to-day (Saturday.) This firm has fully realized the truth of the old saying that "AU work and no play makes Jack a dull boy" and the encouragement which is afforded to wholesehie recreations cannot fail to have good results. There is always a risk in the employment of meta- phors. They are apt to get mixed at times. For instance, at the meeting of the Trades and Labour Council on Tuesday evening a member was declaiming warmly against the inaction of trade unionists on certain local matters. He gave the following extra- ordinary advice :—" Let us go to the Council not like a lamb, but like the wolf and take the bull by the horns !" * * * . .

' The "Soa.pery " has been very generous in the ' dissemination of noxious odours of late, particularly after the " shades of even "have fallen. On Wednes- day night between 10 and 11 o'clock there was a penetrating, pungent, pale purple haze between the bottom of Powys-street and Milner-street which smelt abominably. We really believe, if it had been rain- ing, that the setts would have lathered, for the bad smell doubtless came from good soap. * * * _

Sankey-street is " up." ;,) are many of the trades- men—up in arms. They are not satisfied now that the actual repaving has commenced. It is an inconvenient time and bad for trade and so forth ! Well, someone would have been displeased whenever the work was done. For our part we are delighted to see the excel- lent progress that is being', made in laying the wood- blocks. It is to be hoped they are of a more uniform and durable quality than the last lot. Cheap blocks are the very falsest economy. * * The Cheshire Constabulary took a great interest in the motor cycle trial run from Land's End to John o'Groat's. We hear that on Tuesday evening they turned out in full force in the neighbourhood to witness the passing of the competitors, with a view to trapping the unwary owner who exceeded the time limit. We understand that their vigilance was not rewarded by a single capture. Thus once more has the time-honoured saying "All things come to i him who waits" proved nnacurate.

Our good friend the 'T Warrington Observer" is now quarrelling with Mr. Crosfield, M.P. because he failed to win the Parliamentary golf handicap. Not long since the complaint was that Mr. Crosfield was playing golf when he should have been in Parliament. He has certainly a most difficult task to satisfy some of his constituents. There are people in the town who having given Mr. Crosfield their vote at the last general election, seem to be under the impression that they have bought the Member body and soul. * * The keynote of Mr. Seddon's home policy was hatred of the principle of unlimited competition -the principle of "Every man for himself and the Devil take the hindmost."—" The Times." Mr. Seddon belonged to Lancashire, and Lancashire never sent forth a better example of her peculiar traits. He had the Lancashire directness of speech, the Lancashire energy of mind, coupled with the blunt disregard of the niceties of feeling which is also the attribute of Lancashire.—" Daily News."

* * This is the view of a trade unionist on the Corpora- tion's recent experiment in getting the Markets painted by direct labour recruited from the ranks of unemployed painters : Mr. Grealy (who, we believe, represents the Bakers' Union on the Trades Council) said on Tuesday : "These scabs are our deadly opponents and they have been getting fed out of the rates." What charity and brotherly love between one man and another! In Mr. Grealy's eyes the non- unionist is evidently a social outcast, a being with neither body nor soul worth saving. * * What is your occupation? " was the question asked of a witness at the Warrington County Court on Thursday. " A farmer's son" as the reply, calling forth the remark from Judge Bowen Rowlands: " I should have thought that was his pedigree rather than his occupation." Later it transpired that this same witness had engaged in the unusual occupation of altering the drains at his house and his Honour said " it would have been much better if he had respected the hereditary principle there and employed some person whose father had been a plumber.' * * *
A lady in San Francisco engaged a Chinese cook. When the Celestial came, among other things she asked him was his name.
"My name," said the Chinaman smiling, "is Wang Hang Ho." "Oh, I can't remember all that," said the lady. "I will call you John." John smiled all over and asked, "What your namee ?"

"My name is Mrs. Melville Landon." "Me no memble all that," said John, " Chinantan he no savoy Mrs. t fembel London. Me call you Tommy."—" Tatler." * * * After considerable research we have found out that the aim of the Conservative Workingmen's Federation is "Imperial Federation, whilst actively promoting democratic Conservatism in all its forms." We quite understand what Imperial Federation means. It is the fusion of the Colonies and the Mother Country as one homogeneous whole under the banner of Conservatism The idea seems a simple one, but it has been copy- righted by the Tory, party. A other kind of federation would not be "Imperial" or of any value. But what is " democratic Conservatism ?" This is a hybrid growth we havo not hitherto met With. Perhaps some of our readers can explain. We shall be grateful. * * The famous Ham and Egg Parade at New Brighton is doomed, and we do not suppose anyone will be sorry. £J52,000 is to be spent on a new promenade which will be a credit to the place instead of an eye- sore and a nuisance. It is to be carried from the pierhead right round the front of New Brighton to the western end of the Marine Park, and will thus add three-quarters of a mile to the beautiful Egremont promenade, which at present stretches over two miles, from Seacombe to New Brighton. Eventually, no doubt, the promenade will be carried another three miles, to Leasowe, and when the sea wall is joined up 1 between Hoylake and West Kirby—a gap of about a Imile—the whole of the blunt end of the Wirral Peninsula will be bound in stone and concrete. c-

* * Widnes may. be a " poisonous hell town" but its inhabitants enjoy one advantage—cheap gas. This week the Council decided to reduce the price to the ordinary consumer to is. 3d. per 1,000 cubic feet. Consumers who use the gas for motive power will get it at 11d. per 1,000 cubic feet. Although there are only 5,350 houses in the borough there are 5,683 meters in use. The profit on the gas works during the last year was .£4,703 17s. 4d. Warrington con- sumers are beginning to think that they ought to share to a greater degree in the local gas profits. Relief of rates from this source is very laudable in its way but to the ordinary householder Is. 3d. per 1,000 for his gas sounds even more tempting.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

FOUR GENERATIONS. At the recent annual Whitsuntide processions in Frodsham a curious, and perchance unique, fact pre- sented itself, when four generations were represented among the followers of the Foresters' Society, the patriarch being Mr. Peter Illidge,almost a nonagenarian and the last descendant a little boy of five. POLICE PICNIC. The first detachment of police pic-nicers left Widnes last Thursday morning, and spent an exceedingly pleasant day in the Dukeries. The second detachment visited the same spot on 'Thursday. We regret to learn that an accident befell Miss Strickland, daughter of Superin- tendent R. Strickland, at Penistone, on there turn journey last week. A train backing into the station mounted the platform, demolished a signal and a water column flooding the permanent way. Alarmed at the occurr- ence, Miss Strickland hastily dismounted from her carriage, sustaining a sprained ankle by so doing.

, TWO RUNCORN YOUTHS DROWNED. A FRIEND SACRIFICES HIS LIFE. On Saturday evening Reginald Stanley Booth of Ivy- street, aged eighteen years, and William Clwydfro Williams, of Oxford-road, Runcorn, aged sixteen years, were drowned in the river Weaver Canal in the neigh- bourhood of Frodsham. The event has created a sensa- tion in Runcorn, where the parents and the youths themselves are well-known. It appears that Booth and Williams were members of the Runcorn Boating Club, which has the right to use the Weaver Canal. They rowed some miles from the headquarters at Rocksavage, and then moored their skiff at the bank in order to have a bathe. Williams while yet on the bank, saw that Booth was in difficulties, apparently from cramp, and, with his shirt on, plunged in to the rescue of his friend. This pro'ved beyond his power, and both sank to rise no more. It is stated that neither of the youths had much knowledge or experience of swimming, and the canal is from twelve to sixteen feet deep. A party ot young men from Frodsham grappled for their bodies the whole of Saturday night, and that of Williams was recovered an hour after midnight, and Booth's at three o'clock on Sunday morning. They were conveyed to the Red Lion Hotel at Frodsham to await an inquest. Much sympathy is felt for the grief-stricken parents, as the deceased were manly fellows with good prospects before them. RUNCORN CHURCHMEN AND THE EDUCATION

BILL. On Tuesday night a meeting of Church people of the Runcorn district was held in Runcorn Public Hall to protest against the Education Bill. The Von. Arch- deacon Wood presided over a large attendance. He was supported on the platform by the clergy of the district, the principal church officers, and Messrs. Rigby Swift (barrister-at-law), R. J. MaCartney (Manchester),and Thomas Fielding. Preceding the speaches there was the singing of hymns by the United choirs of the local churches, accompanied by a string band. Prayer was offered by the Rev. C. R. Killick, and then the audience recited the Apostles' Creed —The Chairman said Mr. Birrell informed them that i the new Bill would ost £1,000,000 a year. Mr. Forster, w hen he introduced is Bill in 1870, said that the rate would never be mor than 3d. If they followed pre' cedent, it was likely the cost would be £3,000,000. They were told that the Bill was for the purpose of bringing all education under the same authority, but he was not sure that English people liked monopolies. A monopoly was a dangerous thing, and probably in a number of years to come the Government monopoly of education! would have to be got rid of. The Bill did not give them better education, no better teaching and it did not settle the religious difficulty. This bill was unjust and inequitable, and Churchpeople wanted absolute fair treatment for everybody. The plan to settle the religious difficulty was to pay equally for all, and this he believed was just and practicable. The Archdeacon then moved a resolution protesting against the Education Bill as being in its present form opposed to the first principles of religious equality. Mr. Rigby Swift seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. A resolution pledging the meeting to work for the rejection of the bill was passed on the motion of Messrs. Fielding and Macartney.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GU RDIANS. ALTERATIONS AT THE WORKHOUSE. The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at Dutton on Tuesday when there were present Mr. S. Woodward (presiding) Admiral Jones Parry, Messrs. J. Bolshaw, H. Eyes, G. Egerton Warburton, A. Broome, J. I. Davies, T. Wright, T. Guest, S. Pilling, E. Bretherton, .1. Fryer, J. Spruce, P. Collins, T. Wright.r.J. W. Temperley, J. Hallows, J. Whitley, B. Billington, W. Turner, A. G. Guest and T. Antwis, S. F. Ashton (clerk) andW. E. Hough (assistant clerk).

, ALTERATTO,NS AT THE woußitousu. The Workhouse Alterations Committee reported that Mr. Dancy had made the following recommendations with reference to the proposed alterations at the Work- house : Nurses Home ; kitchen too large but it may remain if a smaller range is put in and the description altered to " dining room." The width of the entrance hall might with advantage be increased from 4 feet 6 inches to 6 feet. Maternity Ward: The architect of the Local Government Board recommends that the roof of this ward be made flat so that it could easily be altered in the event of an extension being desired. Minor alterations were also suggested with regard to the foal ward and the mortuary. Mr. Woodward said that in order to widen the entrance hall at the nurses home it would be necessary to take lft. 31n5. from the kitchen. The committee however did not aocept the suggestion as they felt that the lft. 3inB. was of more value in the kitchen. They quite agreed with the proposal with reference to the roof of the maternity ward. The report of the committee was approved. COST OF OUT-RELIEF,
Mr. Wright reported payments & Out-relief to Mr. Cook £7O, Mr. de Prez 4;30 and Mr. Pearson £25.

The Electricity Supply and Tramways Committee adopted the following report of the sub-committee : "The Clerk reported that as instructed by this Com- mittee, he had addressed circular letters to 292 occupiers of houses and shops (rated at £2O and upwards), and to all the works in the district, inquiring whether they would be willing to take a ' supply of electricity from the Council provided the cost were reasonable, and that the following replies were received :—Favourable for lighting purposes— houses, 30 ; shops, 25 ; church, 1 ; works, 3 ; power, 3-02. Education Committees' Conference. The annual conference of the Association of Educa- tion Committees of England and Wales was opened on Thursday at London'. The Warrington Committee was represented by the Rev. Canon Morley Stevenson, Mr. A. J. Jolley, 'Arr. J. Moore Murray (director of edfication). A resolution approving of the Education Bill was carried by a large majority.

Warrington Child Fatally Scalded. The death has been reported to the police of William Norman, aged one year and five months, son of John Norman, general labourer, 9, Ernest-street. It appears that on Tuesday the mother of the deceased pl aced a can of hot tea on the kitchen table. She had occasion to go into the scullery and during her absence the child pulled over the can, the contents falling on his head and shoulders. He was severely scalded and was at once removed to the Infirmary where he died on Thursday afternoon.
LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AND SHOES, UNDER TEM CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREET.—Advt.. • The Late Mr. John Smith.

The funeral of the late—Mr.-John Smith, (a report of whose death appears on page 7), took place on Thurs- day afternoon at 3 o'clock in the Old Church. Warburton, amid many manifestations of sorrow. There was a large gathering of friends of the deceased gentleman living in and around Warburton, and many others from Latchford, Grappenhall, and Runcorn. The Runcorn Rural District Council was represented by Mr. George Pilling (chairman), Admiral Jones Parry, Mr. S. Woodward (Kingsley), Mr. J. H. Davies (Frodsham), Mr. J. Whitley, 'Mr. G. F. Ashton (clerk), Mr. W. R. do Prez and 'Afr. J. Pearson (relieving officers). and Messrs. J. Douglas and W. M. Morris represented the Runcorn Board of Guardians.

An open meeting was held on Thursday afternoon in Friar's Green Hone. The Rev. H. Wall presided and introduced the Rev. J. F. Matthews, who gave an interesting address. He pointed oat the attention that was being drabn to the evils of intemperanco by posters, and in sonike places by the distribution of circulars among scholol children, which he thought ' would be a good idea to introduce into Warrington. He said that the idea of drinking, either alcohol or ether beverages, was thoroughly imbued in northern nations. At all social junctions, gay or sad, the same custom prevailed, and had done for centuries, so that there was a great weight of inherited taste and I tradition to fight against. He drew attention to the evils of private drinking, and showed that these were often cases where womanly influence would be of great value. After refreshmenis and some charming songs by Miss E. Gilbert, accompanied by Miss Gill, the meeting closed. It is proposed to get up a pic- nic to Eddisbury Lodge in July, and to comn2ariee the members' meetings in the autumn.

Warrington Grammar School. Robert Kennon, a pupil at the Grammaa School, has been awarded after open competitipn a Tate Scholarship of .£35 per annum for 3 years at Liver- pool University. Leigh-street Brass Band.

The Legh-street Brass band played at Manchester on Whit Monday for the Church procession and on the Friday for the Roman Catholics They were warm!) complimented on their smart Playing and attractive uniform by several of the leading officials.

LAWN MOWERS Garden Tools, &c. Splendid selection.—J. S. 'GARLAND, 51, Bridge-st.—Advt. Personal. After absence owing to a lengthy illness his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C., resumed his seat at the Warnngton County Court on Thursday. He was the recipient of the heartiest congratulations from the solicitors present in the Court.

Councillor Wright has this week been discharged from the Delamere sanatorium and has returned to Warrington looking very much better for the treat- ment. Another Brunner Gift to Northwich. At Northwich Urban Council meeting on Tuesday night it was officially reported that Sir John Brunner, M.P., had undertaken to build a new library upon any site to be provided by the Council. The exisiing library, which was Sir John's gift in the Jubilee Year has been condemned owing to a sinking. It was said to have cost £.5.0 Om annum to simply maintain the structure. Water Polo. The sub-committee of the Lancashire County Water Polo Association met in Manchester on Monday, for the purpose of selecting teams for the trial matches at Lancaster on June 16t. and Burnley on June 30th. Amongst the probables to play at Lancaster C. L. Atatton, of the Warrington club, was selected one of the full-backs. div.p: ST HELENS.

ST. HELENS DEPUTY WATER ENGINEER. Mr. A. Willcocks, deputy water engineer of St. Helens, who was married on Tuesday at Belfast, has been presented with a handsome oak clock by the employees of the department. VICAR OF ST. HELENS'S WEDDING. There was a large gathering of members of the St. Helens Parish Church Men's Bible Class on Monday night, when the Rev. Cyril Bardsley, vicar of St. Helens, was the recipient of a set of silver candlesticks, which were presented to him by the members of the class in connection with his forthcoming marriage with Miss Alice Gamble. This happy event takes place next Tuesday at St. Helens Parish Church, when there will be an interesting series of celebrations. WAR ON CO-OPERATION.

ST. HELENS TRADERS TO OFFER A DIVIDEND TO CUSTOMERS. A f ter a lapse of a few years, it would seem that the co-operative war at St. Helens is once more to break out with renewed vigour with the fresh activity which is being shown by the local Traders' Defence Association, a body which sprang into existence during the keen strife of four years ago. The Association have decided toabandon the tactics which they have hitherto employed, and are putting into operation an entirely new scheme by way of fighting co-operation. The experience of the last four years has shown the St. Helens private traders that the people generally will have the dividend on their purchases, whether it comes out of an overcharge or not. They have therefore decided, in order to still further combat the influence of the co-operative society that the St. Helens traders shall band themselves together inaproflt-sharing union. Under the rules of this new association the private traders of the town will, like the local co-operative stores, give a dividend of 2s. in the pound to start with to all customers. The scheme provides that casual cuaoraers [shall receive their dividend by an immediate reduction on the amount of the purchase, while regular customers will be given a dividend coupon. At the end of each week every trader will pay into the bank of the union 10 per cent, of his takings, and each quarter the total amount paid in will be taken out by the secretary and distributed to the holders of coupons from the union's cdntr3l offices. It is hoped by this means to effectually check- mate co-operation, and the privatetraders further claim that the purchasing public will not only be able to receive dividend on their purchases, but, as against the co-operative society, have the distinct advantage which accrues from healthy individual competition. The scheme is to be put into operation immediately the details are settled. The union includes all classes of tradesmen. WRONG MAN CHARGED AT ST. HELENS

" AN EliißESFiillgiAk-E.;; At St. Helens Police Court, on Saturday, the Chief Constable asked leave of the magistrate to withdraw a charge of false pretences which was made a week before I Mr. Ellerington said that a man named Ashourner was charged the previous Saturday with obtaining £5 10s.. by false pretences, and that he had been remanded. A telephone message was received in the even- ing from the police force in North Wales that I they had seen the report of a case in the paper, and they wanted a man for practising the. same kind of fraud as was reported in the St. Helens case. After some conversation with regard to the description of the man they wanted, it was found that the same tactics had been pursued in various places as at St. Helens. Suspicions were then aroused that a case of mistaken identity had occurred. - A photograph of the man wanted by the Welsh police was in the Welsh" Police Gazette," and from one point of view it was somewhat similar to the man who was before their worships and the description was exactly alike in regard to height and other details. After this he felt satisfield that a mistake had been made at St. Helens, and he at once allowed the man out on his own recognisances. He made further enquiries, and he now felt satisfied that the witness had made an honest mistak- in identifying the St. Helens man. Under these cir- cumstances he asked their worships to dismiss the case. The witnesses now felt that they had made a mistake although there was a great similariiy between the two men, and the man in charge was picked out of a number of others by several witnesses ; but there could be no doubt that a mistake had been made by the people who identified the man.—Mr. W. Hutchen appeared on behalf of Mr. Ashburner, and said that if the case had pro- ceeded he could have satisfied them that it was a case of mistaken identity, as his client was a man well con- nected, and he had held a responsible position, and there was no doubt that most grievous harm had been done him, and the probability was that after the case was finished they would have to communicate' with some of the peeple who had been the means of bringing them there. The case had been circulated very freely, and it ' had done the man p considerable amount of harm in St. Helens.—The magistrates at once dismissed the case.

div.head: New Building Schemes.
div.p: New Building Schemes.

The quarterly meeting of the \Carrington Wesleyan Circuit was held at Moore on Thursday when there was a larger attendance than has been known at a summer gathering for some years. The Moore ladies provided an excellent tea. Miss Bessie Dutton acted as hostess. Alderman Bennett suitably expressed the thanks of the meeting to the Moore congregation for their hospitality.

Tiae meeting was presided over by the Rev. Sidney. Pitt who was supported bp the Revs. W. Mellor, J. Manning, A. C. Parker, J. Gannell and J. Howard, Before the business was entered upon, the Rev. J. Gunnell gave a devotional address on : "The personality of the worker." The returns of membership were submitted and considered extremely satisfactory. They showed an increase of 61 for the quarter, the present membership being 867 with 106 on trial. The stewards reported that £95 had been paid into , the bank towards the circuit debt. The income for the quarter it little more than covered the expenditure. The Rev. A. C. Parker leaves the circuit at the end of the ensuing quarter and thanks were expressed to him for his services, warm tributes being paid to his success- ful work at Sankey Bridges and Penketh.

The most important business was the consideration of new building schemes. Three cases came up for approval. Mr. William Bennett has offered to defray the cost of the erection of a spire at Paigate Church in memory of the fact that he has held office in the Wesleyan Methodist Church for fifty years. The offer was very cordially accepted and the meeting signified its consent to the scheme. The Latchford con- gregation asked permission to erect, new schools at a cost of £SOO on the vacant piece of land adjoining the chapel. Two gifts of ,E,lOO each have already been made and the scheme was sanctioned. Permission was also granted for the erection of a new vestry at Sankey Bridges at a cost of £lOO, the whole Of which has already been raised. The Rey. J. Manning presented the Sunday School ' returns, showing that there were 2.763 scholars in the various schools of the circuit (an increase of 4G on the year) with 280 teachers and officers. He also submitted the Day School returns to the effect that at the three lday schools in the circuit there were 1,323 scholars with an average attendance of 1,132. A long discussion took place on the question of foreign missions and there was a strong feeling that some special effort should be made on behalf of the- Westindian fund. It was decided to take a collection in all the churches during the quarter, half of the. amount raised to be devoted to the West Indian lanai and half to the Circuit Debt fund.
The next quarterly meeting will be held at Lymm.on., September 13th.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
CHILD NEGLECT AT WARRINGTON.

At the Warrington Police Court on Monday, James and Mary Harris, of Plerpoint-street,were charged with neglecting four of their children. Defendants appeared before the Court on Friday morning, but owing to their intoxicated condition, they were remanded to the cells until Monday. Mr. Unsworth, who prosecuted for the N.S.P.C.C., stated that Inspector Cox had had the case under his observation for the last 18 months. Both the defendants were habitual drunkards, and the children in consequence were shamefully neglected. The inspector had dealt very leniently with them for the last 12 months, and had given them numerous charxes to reform, but they only cursed him and told him to do what he liked. They had become callous about the matter. Having exhausted all his endeavours to try and make them amend their ways, the Inspector decided to prosecute them. On thr ' sth of June, he visited the house at five o'clock, and found the two defendants and a woman named Melia drinking together. Mrs. Harris was then in a state of intolication, and was nursing her seven-weeks-old baby in such a way that the Inspector was terrified lest she should drop it. She attempted to give it a drink of beer in the Inspector's presence, but he took the bottle away from her. The house was in a very filthy condi- tion, and the bed clothes were nothing but a mass of dirty rags. The other three children came in the house at the time, arid they were shamefully neglected, and were not sufficiently clothed. The cause of the defend- ants' conduct was undoubtedly drink.—Evidence in support of this statement was given by Inspector Cox. The Chief Constable said that if the neighbours were to repeat the stories they had told the police the magis- trates would be horrified. The woman had a long career. Sixteen years ago she was before th court for theft. She had been an habitual drunkard for years and so had her hnsband. They hae simply vied with one another to see which could go down the hill of destruction the faster. He lived in almost daily fear that one would murder the other, or that there would be a big tragedy in the shape of a murder among the children because defendants were drunk every time they had the means. Mrs. Harris had had a month for neglect of children, and another month in 1905 for drnnkenness and using threats. On the latter occasion she attempted to murder her husband when under the influence of drink, but the case was put very mildly.— Both prisoners- denied the neglect.—The Bench fined Harris 20s. and costs (£1 133. lid.) or one month's imprisonment, and Mrs. Harris was sent to gaol for three months without the option of a fine. EMBEZELEMENT AT STOCKTON HEATH.

Edward Farley wee charged at the Daresbury Petty Sessions. on Tuesday, with embezzling the sum of us., the inoneys of his employers, Messrs. R. White and Son, mineral water maul:lecturers, Stockton Heath. —Mr. Browne prosecuted, and said the firm had bad several cases of this description.—The prisoner alleged that a Mr. Collinson, a tradesman, of Frodsbam, had not paid him 2.55., but the firm had Mr. Collinson's receipt. A fresh man was pit on prisoner's round, and it WAS he who found that the money had been paid. The prosecutors would be satisded if a conviction was recorded.—Mr. Steel, for the defence, said he hoped the Bench would agree to the course suggested by Mr. Browne. The defendant merely said he thought the money had not bean paid by Mr Collinson. There was no imputation against Mr Collinson that the account had - not been paid.—The magatrates bound prisoner over under the First Offenders Act, and they hoped it would be a caution to him to be more careful in the f atu re.

div.head: FURIOUS MOTORING NEAR WARRINGTON.
div.p: FURIOUS MOTORING NEAR WARRINGTON.

At Daresbu7 Petty Sessions on Tuesday, William Peach, motor chauffeur, Eden-street, Liverpool, in the employ of Messrs. Lawton and Co., was summoned for driving a motor car at Whitley, on May 19, at a speed exceeding twenty miles an hour.—lt was stated that the defendant on the day in question drove a motor car from Whitley Church to Victoria-square, Stockton Heath, a distance of four and three-quarter miles, in seven minutes. which averaged a speed of forty-one and a quarter miles per hour. Two police officers were stationed at both villages, and booked the number of the car and the time ;t passed, according to the new system adopted by the Cheshire police.—M. T. S. Steel, who defended. admitted exceeding the speed limit, but pleaded that defendant was anxious to get to Warring- ton because it was raining heavily, there being no shelter for the occupants of the car.—The magistrates imposed a tine of £2, including costs.
TIIFFT OE GRMS.-WAREUNGTON RURAL DLiTIZICT
CocNcrL PROSEC UTION.

At the Newton Petty Sessions on Thursday. John Foster, Rodney-street, Warrington, was charged with stealing four gully grids value his, the property of the Warrington Rural District Council.—Mr.Browne, who appeared to prosecute said the District Council desired to press the case as the prisoner's conduct had resulted in considerable danger to persons using the highway. Mr. Browne explained that the grids were seen safe on the highways at Winwick and Parlgate on the 9th bast and were subsequently missed.—P.C. Heath made enquiries and found that they had been broken up and made to look like old iron and then sold to Mr. Toole for s. Prisoner was arrested and had written a con- fession in which he admitted having stolen the grids, and pleaded for leniency.—Prisoner was committed to prison for one month with hard labour.

div.head: AN ARTIFICIAL BEACH'.
div.p: AN ARTIFICIAL BEACH'.
The artificial beach at Grays (Essex) is new nearly completed. Hundreds of tons of sand end shingle have been damped on the Thames side, and already children zire digging as on the "seashore."

div.head: TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL. Letter from Mr. L. R. Crosfield, M.P.
div.p: TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL. Letter from Mr. L. R. Crosfield, M.P.
THE PAINTING OF THE MARKET.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council was held in Bold-street Wesleyan school on Tuesday evening under the presidency of Mr. T. Plumb. There was a small attendance including the secretary (Councillor Stott).

div.head: LETTER FRO3I AIR. A. H. CROSFIELD,
div.p: LETTER FRO3I AIR. A. H. CROSFIELD,

The SECRETLEY read the following letter from Mr, A. H. Crosfleld, M.P.—Hyde Park Hotel, London, May 17th, 190-3. Dear Sir, I duly received your letter of May 9th, and note the resolution passed by the Trades and Labour Council. I have seceived your further letter of May 12th enclosing copy of resolution re•naval stokers new ratings. Will you kindly inform your members that lam in agreement with them on this question and shall act aecordingly when it comes before the House. Yours faithfully, A. H. Crosaeld." Councillor STOTT remarked that on this occasion no one could complain of the length of the letter. GREAtY : tIONV is he attending to his duties now? , Councillor .hTorr : I think he is doing all right. Mr. PLLNSTON (to Mr. Grealy) : Your medicine has done him good. Th 3 matter then dropped.

div.head: WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE.
div.p: WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE.
The Plums MINISTJER acknowledged the receipt of a resolution from the Council in favour of women's suffrage. , • THE PAINTING On THE MARKETS, DISSATISFACTION WITH TETE COUNCIL'S CONDUCT.

Councillor STOTT read the report prepared by the Borough Surveyor on the painting, of the markets by direct employment of labour and said he considered it to be an excellent one and very satisfactory from the Trades Council's standpoint. Some of the men employed had not handled a paint brush for a considerable time and when they also considered the difficulty of prevent- ing damage to goods and having to remove the scaffold- ing twice a week, the work had been very well accom- plished. There was only one tender lower than the actual cost and he was convinced that if the Council could have taken twelve men from a trade union branch who were in practice and kept them continuously employed, the work would have been done even better. He hoped that the Markets Committee and other com- mittees of the Corporation would try to carry all their painting out by this direct method. It would bea great deal better for the ratepayers and the workingmen. All the men employed received the standard rate of wages. Mr. COECHIN, the delegate of the Painters' Society, moved a vote of thanks to Councillor Stott for the interest he had taken in the matter. The scheme had perhaps not worked out exactly as they would have liked it, seeing that their society paid about £2OO in out-of-work pay last winter. Nevertheless they were, indebted to Councillor Stott for his action. Mr. T. SMITH said that all he was afraid of was that the system would give non-payers to trade societies more privileges than it gsve the benefit members. If that were the case, the contributions to trade unions would be reduced.

Mr. Collars pointed out that the best members of their societies did not like to sign the Distress Com- mittees books, although they had been advised to do so. Consequently the" fag" end of the trade would prob- ably get the work first. Councillor STorr said that difficulty was not lost sight of, but he felt it would not justify his position to make I objections while the work was being done. He wanted the Council to try it as an experiment. lied the trade unionists begun to complain the Council Would have said : "We will have no more direct employment." If similar work were again undertaken by the Council he hoped the trade unionists would register their names at the Labour Bureau, as under the new system it was no indignity to do so. Mr. GREALY thought trade unionists ought to have had the preference. He failed to see the advantage to trade unionists of the Council having done the work directly. Mr. MASSEY said the Labour bureau was going to cut trade unionists down. Influence ought to be brought to bear to get the Town Council to employ none but trade union labour. The CHAIRMAN said the labour bureau was no remedy for unemployment but only a paliative. Before trade unionists could get their rights work would have to be provided for 'everyone. It would be difficult to get the Town Council as at present constituted to employ only trade unionists. If they had a majority of labour members they might persuade them to do so. Mr. CORALS said that three at least of the contractors mentioned by Mr. Longdin were trade union employers. Mr. • GREALY : I think the Markets Committee ought to be censured. These scabs (non-unionists) are our deadly opponents and they have been getting fed out of the rates. _ _ _

Councillor Srorr asked if it was not better for the Corporation to experiment on the lines they had done —even though it had been a disadvantage to the Painters' Society—than to ran any rizak of private contractors employing boys instead of qualified workmen. They had no guarantee if the work had been let out to con- tract that half as many trade unionists would have been employed. There was of coarse a danger of the labour bureau, if it was not watched, being mod to furnish employers with cheap labour. They could not reason- ably expect Corporation Committees as at present constituted to give preference to trade union labour. The Painters' Society sent in the names of three men whom they considered suitable for the post of Clerk of Works but the committee would not accept them as coming from a trade union branch butonly as individuals. Mr. PLINSTON thought part of the discussion was, likely to detract from the good step taken by the Cor- poration and he was rather sorry the remarks had been made. Looking at the matter through trade union spectacles al.me he agreed with the remarks of Mr, Greal y and others, but they bad to bear in mind that Councillor Stott had brought about a move such as had never been taken in Warrington before. He had gained a certain principle and it would be much easier to improve on that and obtain conditions which trade unionists desired than it would have been if Councillor Stott had raised those objections at the time the step was being taken. Let them be careful in dealing with the Town Council constituted as it was, that, they did not at the outset damage the cause. Mr. Massuy did not like this milk and water system," and the Council ought to fight it to the end, even though it might damage the cause for the time being. If a Councillor did anything to injure him as a trade unionist he became his bitter enemy. He admired the way in which the painting of the markets had been done, but he maintained that as long as trade unionists paid into their societies to keep up the price of their labour, they ought to see that trade unionists were employed. Mr. PODNIORE said the principle of trade unionism was one of thrift, carefulness and judicious thought for the future and as such ought to command the support of any Councillor. If the trade unionists of Warrington would make up their minds to fight every ward with a sterling, honest man, who would stand only for Labour, they could alter things in twelve months. But the trade unionists of Warrington were too selfish in this respect. Until they had sunk all minor matters of, difference and resolved to work for the common good, he had not the slghtest hope of ever benefiting trade unionism or Labour. He hoped the Unemployed Act would be so altered as to guarantee the right of employ- ment to the people of this country. Mr. Wit.r.lamsost moved that tt„e meeting should thank Councillor Stott but express its regret that the Town Council could not see its way to employ only trade union labour on the work. This resolution was sez.onded by Mr. GREALY and lagreed to. THE LABOUR REPRESENTATION COMMITTEE THE QUESTION OF AMALGAMATION. '

Mr. GREALY said he thought the local Labour Representation Committee was making poor progress as many societies did nqt seem to support it. He sug- gested that the organizdtion could be better worked if It were amalgamated with the Trades Council, and it wonld be a giant advantage to the cause of Labour. Mr. CORRN said that in Halifax the Labour Repre- sentation Committee and Trades Council worked together. The change required in Warrington was that the Trades Couqcil should work politically and not con- fine itself to ordi wiry monthly meetings. Councillor SToTT said the Council had always taken politio4 action since be could remember. It was not the fault of the Labour Representation Committee that that committee had not been successful, but of th:! rank nod file of the trade union nranches. At present there was too much overlapping in the work of the Trades Council and the Labour Representation Committee. The SECRETARY was instructed to obtain information as to the arrangement in vogue at Halifax. j PROGRESSIVE LABOUR LEAGUE AND " RIGHT

div.head: TO 'WORK" COMMITTEE.
div.p: TO 'WORK" COMMITTEE.

Councillor grorr said he bad received a letter from Mr. Morton, secretary of the Progressive Labour League, stating that the organization had discussed the question of the local" Right to ‘Vork " Committee and had appointed five delegates to represent them on the committee. He asked to be informed as to the time of the first meeting. The letter rather startled him (Councillor Stott) and some of the delegates thought he had been in communication with the League, but that was not so. He replied to Mr. Morton that he would be exceeding his duties if he invited any organization outside the three concerned in the formation of the committee to send delegates. At a meeting of the committee the same views were expressed and it was decided that it be left to the Trades Council, Independent Labour Party and Labour Representation Committee to say whether it was desirable to accept representatives from the Lesgne. The names submitted by the League were : Meters. Thomas Barnes, Samuel Wright. Joseph Elwell, Rev. H. Dunnico and Mr. Morton (secretary). I Mr. Courtly : Has it been suggested to admit representatives from the Conservative Club? The SECRETARY : You can't suagest anLthing yet. The matter was adjourned for a month. 1 •

div.head: ENCOURAGEMENT FROM WARRINGTON.
div.p: ENCOURAGEMENT FROM WARRINGTON.
GRAVEL PUMPED LIKE WATER.

Pumping gravel like water through a large iron pipe /may seem a strange and unique pro- ceeding, but this is what is actually done in cer- tain districts in Indiana. A 6in. pump is used, driven by a 1511.-p. engine, and three men are necessary for its operation. A plant of this kind has a capacity for lifting 100 yards of gravel a-day.

div.head: ORIGINAL MICROPHONE.
div.p: THE ORIGINAL MICROPHONE.

A hint to inventors, who chronically complain that they cannot find the funds to demonstrate their inventions, is to be found in a statement recently made by Lord Rayleigh, concernin Hughes, the father of many important electrical inventions, upon whom he had called in his lodg- ings one night, and was shewn his invention of the microphone, now substantially used for tele- phoning. Hughes had no apparatus at all. A few match-boxes, a stick or two of sealing-wax, sonic nails and a single cell of a battery made up in a bedroom tumbler constituted the mate- rial of his invention.

div.head: TEMPERATURE .OF ADULTS.
div.p: THE TEMPERATURE .OF ADULTS.

The ordinary temperature of an adult when a thermometer is placed in the armpit is 98•4 deg.; in the mouth, 99.5 deg.; the blood is about 100 deg. Blood heat is marked on the thermo- meter at 99deg.Fahr. In fevers this is much ex- ceeded, and the heat of the patient may rise to 105 deg. or 106 deg.; a higher temperature than this will generally prove fatal, unless it descend soon: The highest temperatures recorded have been in some case i of rheumatic fever, when that of the body rose to 109 deg., and even tib. 111 deg.

div.head: MEASURING PAIN.
div.p: MEASURING PAIN.

A new branch of science is named Dolorime- try, and its function is the " measurement " of the dynamics of pain by material means. The process is the "invention of M. W. Serieyx, who has been moved to study the subject by the ter- rible extent to which cruelty towards horses is daily witnessed in the Paris streets. His theory is that though French drivers and others in charge of horses are brutal towards the animals, they are really more . stupidly ignorant than malignant, and he has developed Dolorimetry as a means of giving them the evidence of their own eyes of the grave physical effects of cruelty. The dolometer shows that the dynamic force of a sharp _cut with an ordinary carter's whip is equal to about 2851 b., and that a vigorous jerk at the reins puts a pressure of about 3051 b. on the horse's head. M. Serieyx thinks that if they can be. made acquainted with these figures horse- men will be more careful. ATOMS THAT NEVER VANISH.

The "indivisible atom " in some cases disinte- grates; the radium atom, for instance. At- tempts are being made to measure the rate at which atoms are disintegrating—if they are. Sir William Ramsay has said: "It has often been stated that for a quantity of radium to dis- appear to half its weight takes about 1,100 years. It is always half itself that disappears in that period, so that when half has gone, half the re- mainder will disappear in another 1,100 years, and half the remainder in a similar number of years, and so on ad infinitum. For that reason we say, 'when it is half gone' and pot 'when it is gone.' If you are eating bread and butter, and consume half a slice in ten minutes, and half the half slice in another ten minutes, and half the remainder in a like period, ,and so on, you will go on for ever. It is the old theory of planing the plank. So long as you do not take away more than half the thickness of the plank you will always hate something to plane at.

div.head: VIOLENT DEATHS.
div.p: VIOLENT DEATHS.

Severe injuries to the body are seldom very painful at first. The severity of the nervous shock seems to paralyse the nerve centres where i consciousness of pain is situated, and n fatal cases there is oven no sense of pain, even when death is delayed a day or two. In such cases, says Health, .it may be supposed that the shock no longer paralyses but even destroys the nerve centre. It may be compared to a lightning flash along the telegraph wires. Although of the same nature as the electric telegraph current, yet it is so intense ,as to destroy the receiving instru- ments, so that no subsequent message can be re- ceived. In smile fatal inj, i uries, t he nerve that would carry the pain to tne brain s destroyed, and such accidents are almost painless. Our i sense of pain is greatest n the skin, and deep wounds are, therefore, not more veprayitnhfeupl painful, h slight ones. In surgical operations the skin in- ciasniod, so n isonfleten fatal minltriepsainafurel; On especially those that interfere with breathing, such as injuries to the chest and throat.

div.head: "THE SHADOW OF THOUGHT."
div.p: "THE SHADOW OF THOUGHT."
,A44i

_ A curious report comes. from New York to the effect that Professor Elmer Gates, of Washington, has discovered that ultra-violet light of a certain wave-length penetrates dead' material easily, while living tissue obstructs it. In other words, in this invisible light—which can be made manifest to the eye by various means—a living substance will cast a shadow, while the same substance dead will not do ,so. Professor Gates is said to have repudiate's] the idea that the shadow cast is that of the soul, and he attributes it to the presence of electric currents in nerves and muscles of living tissues. These currents being absent when the tissue is dead, ultra-violet light passes unimpeded and no shadow is cast. According to the report, it is hoped that this discovery will prove an im- portant means of diagnosis in various diseases, supplementing the valuable evidence afforded by the X-rays; and it is said to furnish the only reliable means of ascertaining in certain cases whether death has or has not actually taken place.

HEAT-RESISTING MATERIALS. The extreme temperatures necessary in modern industries have developed a new kind of engineering work in the selection of materials that are adapted for containing vessels and utensils by their resistance to booth heat and chemical action. Reviewing the refractory sub- stances available, M. Auguste Morel, a French engineer, finds carbon in the form of graphite, to be especially valuable, as it resists almost all temperatures, but it unites chemically with iron, and cannot be used in work with that metal. Pure silica is very useful,. though it softens in the oxyhydrogen flame and unites with alkalies. More resistant still is alumina, which fails only in the electric furnace, and resists all such cor- rosive actions as oxide of iron, to which silica yields. Chalk, though very subject to chemical action, withstands heat wonderfully. Magtiesia, titanic acid, and iron oxide are other simple natural compounds, but the electric ,furnace is producing many complex manufactured mate- rials—like ,arborundum—that are taking their place for practical purpdses. In working with great heat the electric furnace offers an enor- mous advantag,, as the intensest heating is in- ternal, and substantes can be acted upon by temperatures that would destroy the crucible walls if -applied from the outside.
SOME PROPERTIES OF LIQUID NITROGEN.

- - The properties of liquid nitrogen have been Izss exhaustively studied than those of liquid oxygen, and in a German chemical magazine H. Erdmann contributes some interesting data with reference to the former of these liquefied gases. Liquid nitrogen is a very limpid, perfectly i colourless fluid, thus differing n colour from the blue liquid air. Fragments of ice sink in liquid nitrogen, and so also does frozen alcohol, al- though at first the liquid spirit remains on the surface buoyed up by the rapidly-volatilised nitrogen. Liquid ozone diffuses only slowly into liquid nitrogen, but the two substances when shaken together form a clear, blue solution. At first sight liquid nitrogen seems to be as chemi- cally inert as the gas itself, and extinguishes even a glowing magnesium ribbon. A mixture of finely divided calcium and liquid nitrogen Famot be made to combine by ordinary pro- -cess. When, howevex, the mixture is fired by a priming, as in the thermite process, an ener- getic reaction occurs throughout the mass, which glows and emits sparks and becomes transformed into calcium nitride. This product, ‘when treated with water, evolves a copious stream of ammonia gas.

If this sphere is filled with matters suspended in water the results vary in accor- dance with whether such substances are heaNder or lighter than the fluid in which they, are in snspension. In the former case they arrange themselves agaimt the, glass in each helmisphere between two ,planes parallel with the equator, placed symmeirically above and .bolow it; in the latter they constitute a column' occupying the position of the axis. The heavier particles in the first case collect in the space between the above planes and are arranged on the boundaries of the zone of the cohere marked out by them: tee parvicies ugnter man water are rouna in ins position where the movement is least, which is represented by the anis of rotation. • These re- sults, of coarse. comments the Times, agree g - tirely with theory.,

And when that temporary home was found, But, thanks to Doan's backache kidney pills, I am to know ' I free from these troubles now, and I am indeed grateful that even then no fire could be lighted! There are. few Doan's Backache Kidney Pills. families in San Francisco to-day but what can talk byl the hour of incidents the most harrowing that have happened in their own little Circles. When the quake had made it impossible for the people to remain in their homes they fled to the hills and the park. When a bit calmer, 1 turned to the difficult task of finding a waggon with which to convey my belongings across the bay. A frightened,trembling crowd it was that threaded its way through the debris on its way to the ferry boats. Since writing the above I have received a Welsh paper containing what I suppose Will be the general i report sent by the Press Association to English speak- ' ing papers. The report is fairly correct with the exception of the statement of the number of lives lost. The number the Coroner passed a verdict upon may reach 700, and to this we may add the likelihood of al number none can count or guess at that would be killed ; and burned, leaving no trace. The owners of I waggms very soon found it was harvest time I to them. I paid down ' £ll before the man would lift a hand, and then I had to keep • close watch to see that he did not drive off and deposit my goods where he could find them another day. Hundreds of cases there were of people losing all they had and not through quake or fire. Quite a number of our own acquaintances left their homes and fled to the hills. They were not so fortunate as we. In our case, on our return we found all much as we left it, but several of our friends found their homes cleared ont,—the thieves had keen. Thieves abounded and martial law practically existed and "shoot on sight " was the order. All saloons were closed, and the corner groceries were closed after their stores of liquor had been emptied into the gutters. The regular soldiers, marines, and the militia took possession of the wretched city and the citizens had to obey. To get back to my waggon. What we saw when we reached the ferry was 'a bewildering situation. The boats were being loaded as fast xts possible, • but it seemed awfully slow work, and it was only after a long wearying wait that my truck got on board. I started to count the number of conveyances on the boat. That is, teams of three horses like mine, of two horses, and of one, with a thick sprinkling of automobiles. I counted up to sixty and then gave it up. This, in addition to the dense crowd that filled the upper deck, made up a cargo of animate and inanimate, that was repeat. edly carried across the bay to Oakland, Berkley, and Alameda. As may well be supposed it was soon impossible to find an empty house, and rents went sky high. I should think that at least 200,000 people left the city. The railways offered every facility to the people to escape from what seemed to be a doomed city, even carrying them free across the I continent into the eastern states. The above is a brief sketch of our quitting San Francisco. It is just five weeks since the big tremblers gave us a sample of what could be done in the way of lifting buildings, and lam right in saying the nervous excitement has not abated one jot, especially among the ladies. It may be that we shall go back some day to live again in San Francisco, but just now at least two of my family are more inclined to quit the State, with or without leave, than to think of making a permanent residence anywhere within its borders. We are living with some good friends, and, I fear, we thall have to / do for a long time, for there are no houses to be had. All went down in the city in the districts in which rents were considered reasonable. The town in which we are placed at present is a most beautiful one. Fields, flowers, and green trees abound. What a change from the great noisy city, with its bell ringing cars ! Our city did not feel the worst effects of the quake. Take the city as the centre of a radius of fifty miles, and there are numerous small towns where the buildings were chiefly of wood that are complete wrecks, and this without the aid 'of fire. When one thinks of all that this means, of the wreck of the home, of the sudden stoppage of the income, it is simply pitiable. In my small circle there are a number of friends who in less than two minutes were reduced to'almost abject poverty. Not a stick, nor even a bite of bread. Not even a job to work at.' In my opinion the most pitiable cases are to be found among those who never did any hard work. It is hard to tell a well-educated clerk to go into the shed and shovel at the heaps of rubbish, or to take a hatchet and clean bricks, and just now there are hundreds of blistered fingers. The authorities are doing all they can to provide clothing for those who have lost all, and to give food where there is no money to buy with,but the task is a difficult one,and the organiz- ing of a commisary able to cope with the greedy and selfish and to see that the needy and shy get what is needed seems almost impossible. If the usual long spell of dry weather takes it usual course the tent- dwellers will not suffer much. The Insurance Societies may make things unpleasant by withholding money. Immense sums are needed at once so that the rebuild- ing of the city can place work within reach of the 1-colliers. Another feature is, so many of the workers have left the city. The brick-layers are now receiving 2s. day, and their helpers are paid 10s. This and an eight hours day iPt given as an inducement to workmen to return to the city. It is a mistake for any one to say that wooden buildings stand the shock of earthquake the best. The big steel structures stood the test the best. The warehouse I was in, when the shock came, was all wood, the bolts and nails being about the only iron I knew of, yet when the electric light suddenly went Out and I after much searching, found a door the building had been shaken out of shape and it was only after much difficulty I got out of the building at all. The hospital in which my youngest daughter is a nurse, was built entirely of wood but it became a wreck. Fortunately for her she was on night duty. The roof, chimney and wall went through her bed to the floor below. As I have said it is five week:s since the quake yet I have not seen the girl, and don't know when I shall; the nurses are kept so busy. The number pf hair breadth escapes that have come to my knowledge are very numerous and very start- ling. One young lady acquaintance when roused by the shock sat up in bed and at once the chimney and part of the wall went through the pillow behind her to the floor below. In another case the husband had just left the bedroom when the shock came, and the roof and chimney fell through the bed grazing the wife's arm and doing no further harm to her. I might state, to show the force of the shock, that my daughter the nurse was walking along the corridor, and she waslso battered from wall to wall that her finger ends were all blistered and bad to be wrapped up. We may forget the fire, but we shall never forget the earthquake of April 18th, 1900. H. WHITHAM. May 23rd, DK

div.head: [By Mr. H. Whithaw].
div.p: [By Mr. H. Whithaw].
THIRTEEN A SIDE.
IMPORTANT NORTHERN UNION CHANGES.
Touch-Rule Altered.

The annual meeting of the Northern Rugby Football Union took place on Tuesday night at the George Hotel, Huddersfield. It was presided over by Mr. J. H. Smith, the president, and was attended by some sixty representatives of clubs affiliated. First on the agenda wEre some amendments to the government of the Union but they were not carried. THIRTEEN v. FIFTEEN A SIDE.

It was as affecting the laws of the game, however, that the chief proposals were made. A proposition of the Warrington Club, backed by Leigh, was that the game should be played by thirteen players, instead of fifteen, and a further amendment to reduce the number to twelve was proposed by Whitehaven Recreation, seconded by Wath Brow, while St. Helens suggested fourteen as the conatitution of a side. Mr. H. Ashton, 6f Warrington, argued that to play thirteen men would yield a better game, would make it much faster, and enable a better system of formation in the scrummage. In addition it would, he said, mean a saving of fully £lOO a year to ninny clubs. Mr. J. Lewtlawaite (flunslet) thought it would be much better if a team played seven 'forwards and six I backs.

Mr. J. B. Cooke (Wakefield Trinity) expressed him- self Ls strongly in favour of the proposal—not because of the saving, but because it would open out the game, and, in his opinion, result in a marked improvement. He did not, he said, know a single instance in which clubs running a workshops' competition had had teams of more than twelve players a side. Mr. F. Lister (Halifax) called attention to the game played at Headingly between the New Zealanders and Yorkshire as showing what fine football could be pro- duced with fifteen aside. _
Mr. McCutcheon, of Oldham, favoured the playing of seven forwards and six ba.ck. _

There were 43 votes in favour of the change and 18 against it. so that it was agreed to, amid applause. Whitehaven's proposal in favour of twelve players was defeated by a large majority, and the St. Helens' suggestion in favour of fourteen met a similar fate. SEQUEL TO A ILEADINGLEY EPISODE. Law 3 provided that a referee having given his decision after blowing his whistle cannot under any circumstances alter it.' To this rule Mr. J. W. Wood, on behalf of the Leeds Club, proposed to add the words "except as to touch and touch-in-goal play." The reason for this suggested change emanated from the occurrence that took place at the Leeds v. Broughton Rangers Cup-tie at Headingley, when it was alleged that the referee, having allowed a try, afterwards altered his decision because the touch-judge's flag bad been raised. The proposal was, however, withdrawn. PLAYING_ THE 13A1.L. .

_ Proposals in the name of the Bradford Club, seconded I by the Bradford and District Union, provided in effect for a return to the "play the ball " rule, and for the I ," line out." In regard to the former, the sponsors of the new rule had the support of the Union Committee, in proposing that 'instead of a scrummage when a player had bean tackled he "shall at once put the ball down in front of him between himself and his opponents' lgoal line." In support of the change it was argued 1 that if it was introduced continuity of movement would be secured, such as made the play of the New Zealanders so attractive.,On the other hand, it was said that to "play the ball" was often highly dangerous. There were 89 votes for the change, and 17 against it ; so that it was agreed to. The following proposal, as an addition to Law 8, was lost in the case of the breaking up of a scrummage and he forwards dribble away in a body,, the game shall not be stopped for accidental offside play on the part of such forwards, notwithstanding the method of pro- cedure otherwise provided for unintentional offside play. A proposal to prevent players approaching within ten yards of one receiving the ball, as against the present rule of five yards, was defeated. The following addition was unanimously made to Law 11:—" The referee may refrain from putting the provisions of this law into effect in cases where he is satisfied that by enforcing them he would be giving an advantage to the opposing side." With a view to securing a good, 'Compact scrummage it was unanimously resolved that a penalty might be impo.,ed if any player or team Wilfully and systematically endeavours to prevent the formation of a fair and properly-formed scrummage." THE SUBJECT OF TOUCH PL4Y. The subject of touch play, in regard to which several suggested changes stood on the paper, caused a good deal of discussion. A variety of opinions was given !expression to, showing almost I general dissatisfaction wth the present system of' scrummaging ten yards out. A proposal from Bradford in favour of a reversion to the old „line-out met, however, with very poor support and it was lost. Tenb end tho following resolution, proposed by Oldham, alid seconded by Wakefield Trinity was agreed to The ball is in touch when it or a player carrying it touches or crosses the touch line. When the ball drops directly into touch it shall (except in a case of a penalty kick) be brought back and scrummaged at the spot 4om whence it was kicked ; in all other cases it shall taken into play ten yards from and at right angles ; to the touch line, and there put down and scrummaged.

div.head: WEAK, DIZZY, NO APPETITE. A Hastings Woman Cured of "Pains Like Knife Stabs," by Mother Seigel's Syrup.
div.p: WEAK, DIZZY, NO APPETITE. A Hastings Woman Cured of "Pains Like Knife Stabs," by Mother Seigel's Syrup.

There is no healthier spot in England than Hastings. But there are some ailments upon which climate has little or no effect, prominent among them being indigestion and biliousness; and so it happens that Mrs, Emily klootroani of 5, Bravbrooke Terrace, Hastings, writes thus on January 24th, 1905: "It is about seven years since my health broke down. I found myself in low spirits, without appetite, and lacking interest in everything. Gradually this feeling increased ; my digestion broke down, so that I became afraid of food of whatever kind. There was a constant sensation of pressure at the chest, with sharp pains like stabs of a knife, darting through my back. Sometimes these pains came on while I was in the street, so acutely that I could not refrain from crying gut. "Wind in my stomach and bowels was another of my troubles ; it was constant, and I was rarely free from headache. Heart palpitation, if not so frequent, was more alarming, and so interfered with my sleep that for two years or mored did not knvy what a proper night's rest was. Each morning fonnd me dizzy and rturefreshed. '‘ Giving up solid food for ntime,l lived upon liquids; hut this caused more wind and pressure than ever. I became thin and neak from want of food, and the dizziness increased so that when in the street I had to stop every now and then and press my hand over my eyes to steady myself. ' "After a doctor had treated me for two years without the least benefit, I turned to Mother Seigel's Syrup,and began a course of that medicine. There was an improve- meat at once in my condition. It seemed to remove the load from my chest. That improvement continued !until soon I had neither pain nor palpitation, my diges- tion was sound, and I was in all respects as well as ever I had been in my life." ' -

div.head: "DIE BEFORE LIE."
div.p: "DIE BEFORE LIE."

A little ragged boy was once found on board an outward steamer that had left port some days. He was brought to the first mate and asked to point out the cheat who had smug- gled him on board. The boy replied that his step-parent did it as he could not afford to keep him, and so desired to send him to a rich aunt abroad. The mate did not credit the story, in spite of the boy's honest face, for he had heard similar tales that were not true. He 'thought the sailors had plotted to help the boy away, eo he dealt hardly towards him repeatedly, and called him 'bad names. Thia went on day by day, but in spite of all the boy could lit be got to blame the sailors. At last the mate, who was tired of the boy's story, took him by the throat and dragged him to the ikon- deck. There he pointed to the highext mast and told the boy that he should han.glhere in ten minutes unless he told a true tale. The people on board gathered round, and in the midst knelt the boy, while the mate stood in front to take the time. It was one of the finest sights', said a witness, that he had ever beheld, Lo see the pale, wasted face of that noble boy, who resolved to meet death sooner than lie. As soon as eight minutes had fled the mate told him that he had only two minutes more to live unless he gave a true story. The boy answered, "I cannot lie; I should like to pray." The mate nodded his head, turned pale, and shook like a reed in the wind. And there the little fellow knelt and begged that God might receive him if he died. A scene that touched all hearts then took place; the mate sprang forward and hugged the boy to his breast.. He blessed the boy, and told him that he at last credited his story, and that ,while he lived he should not want a friend.
Now I will close, hoping you are in perfec health.—l remain, your affectionate member, H. M. DITIBTJET.

div.head: DON'T.
div.p: DON'T.
Don't snub a boy because he Wears shabLy clothes—Witen Edieon, the inventor of the telephone, first entered Boston, he w.ore a pair of yellow linen breeches in the depth of winter.
Don't snub a boy because his house is plain and unpretending—Abraham Lincoln's early home was a log cabin.
Don't snub a boy because of the ignorance of bis parents—Shakespeare, the world's poet, was a son of A man who was unable to write hie own name.
Don't snub a boy because he chooses a humble trade—The author, of "Pilgrim's Pzogress" was a tinker.

Don't :snub a boy because of a physical dis- ability—Milton was blind. Don't snub a boy because of dulness in hit+ lessons—Hogarth, the celebrated painter and engraver, was a stupid boy at his books. Don't snub a boy because he stutters—Demos- thenes, the greatest orator of Greece, overcame a harsh• and stammering voice. - Don't snub any one. Not only because some day he may far outstrip you in the race of life, but because it is neither kind nor right nor Christian.
‘I remain, your affectionate niece, JANIE HOLT.

Pretty Polly Popkins sat down upon rt. z:eol, Wouldn't learn her lessons, and wouldn't go to 'school; Her pother loved her dearly, but thoulit :t . , was quite sad . That little Polly Popkins should be so very bad.

Polly's cheeks were rosy, and. Polly's eyEswere blue, Polly's golden ringlets hung down straight and true; Polly's feet were nimble, and won full many a race; . But a frown of angry trouble hid the beauty of her face.

"Don't like nasty sums," said she; "don't like 14asty books; ' Let me go to play; mamma, by the running brooks; Bessie Brown's come home, mamma, for a holi- day, Let me stay at home with her; please do let me stay!"
No, dear," said her mother, better go; Your holidays will soon be here, I really must say Dry your pretty eyes, Polly, give me a bweet kiss, I'm glad you are not often a naughty gir! like this."

A BROKEN HEART.

A little china figure On a little bracket sat. His little feet were always crossed, He wore a little hat;' And every morning, fair or foul, In shine or shadows dim, A pretty little housemaid came And softly dusted him.

• . She took him up so gently, And with such a charming air, His china soul was melted quite; : loved her to despair. !lay he sat and thotght of her ntil the twilight came, And in his china dreams at night, He breathed her little name.

One day, while being dusted,, In his joy he. trembled so, To feel her little fingers that, Alas! she let him go; ' In vain she tried to grab him back, Fate /willed it they should part; He fell against the fender edge, And broke his little heart.

She gathered up his fragments, And sheNtold a little he, Expounding to her mistress how The cat had made him die; And on the following morning, when The shutters back she thrust, She spoke his little epitapla " Therels one thing less to dust."
