Three Important Developments.

Such is the • title of an article in the special "Coming of Age" issue of the 'lrish Cyclist,' a delightful production, full of reviews and remi- niscences of the past two decades. The three most important developments were all old ideas re-invented. The • first, of Course, was the pneumatic tyre originally invented by Thompson In 1845, but found a failure. . Re-invented by Mr. Dunlop in 1888, it proved an unqualified success, not only revolutionizing and extending cycling,, but rendering possible for pleasure purposes the motor vehicles of the present day. Next in importance came the variable speed gear, in the compact, light form of the hub tyre, Invented by Mr. Reilly. 'Although the idea of variable gears was exploited in the early eighties on heavy tricycles, it was not until the mechanism assumed its modern form that it became a general boon and. a commercial success. The third development was the revival of the free wheel, common on the early tricycles alluded to above, but only resusci- tated by a mere accident. The makers of the once famous Whippet bicycle had a variable gear actuated by back pedalling, which necessitated a clutch drive.. Several buyers took a fancy to the "free wheel" without being enamoered of the gear, and so the fashion caught on. To Mr. C. A. Hyde belongs the redit of designing the perfect .Flutch that bears his name. The free wheel brought with it the universal adoption of efficient rakes to each wheel. The Growth of Cycle Camping. Some idea of the progress of cycle camping, since Mr. T. H. Holding published his Cycle and Camp,' about •eight years ago, may be gleaned from the estimate that there are now some 600 cycle campers in the country, each possessed of a complete equipment averaging 12 lb. in weight, which enables them to tour at home or abroad, at pleasure, the tost of living being about 13e. a week. The A4Sociation of Cycle Campers has lately published a—list of tents and accessories at much reduced prices. The fact that the early votaries of camping had to make their own tents and appliances is an eloquent. proof of their enthusiasm. At the recent competition at the Crystal Palace, a special prize was offered for equipment and neatness of kit, and was won by a lady, Miss E. B. Wallace. Special ingenuity was shown in the attachmerit of the stove to the frame, a minor prub:cm of difficulty. The first prize of £2 2s. for tent pitching, was carried off by Mr. FL I: en Steele, the Hon. Sec., Mrs. Horsfield being a good se-I•or.d. Another contest required the camper to light his stove and boil a pint of water. The site being somewhat exposed, this proved a difficult feat, bat the winner, Mr. F. 'G. Snowdon, boiled his pint in 4 min. 50 sec.

div.head: Mr. J. E. Warren and the Northern
div.p: Mr. J. E. Warren and the Northern
Union.

Warrington's only football success daring the season 1905-6 was recorded by the " A " team who secured the championship of the Lancashite Rugby Combination. On Friday night the Members of the team, together, with the first team players and the oHicials of the club were entertained to dinner at the Lion Hotel, in cele- bration a the victory. An excellent repast was served and the proceedings throughout were of an enjoyable nature. . .

Mr. J. E. WARREN, president of the club, in present- ing the championship medals to the "A " team said it perhaps seemed rather singular that a committee pledged to economy should at its first meeting resolve to spend money on junketing but he hoped the members of the club would regard it in the proper light because they must all agree that the " A " team thoroughly deserved every little recognition which could be given to them. The "A " team had been the only section of the Club which during the past season had upheld the honour of the Club. he regarded a god second line as a most valuable asset and he was sorry that some of the Lancashire, Clubs were dropping their "A " teams with a view to economy, althormh he regarded it as a false economy. (Bear, hear;) Ile strongly depricated the action of some of tke Yorkshire clubs, in allowing Rugby and Association matches to be alternately played on their grounds. lle never could understand such a fatuous policy , and could never appreciate why a Rugby Club should allow the A:sociation code t be cultivgted as in the end it only resulted in their own throats being cut. With regard to the Northern Union it was., desir- able that they should get a re-constructed conunittee. When it WAS inaugurated the Union had a I membership of 10 clubs, and although it had grown the committeni F., till consisted of representatives from Id clubs onlv. In order to make the Union successful the ' basis of the committee must be broadened, and the body must be popularly elected and not as at 'present for each of the members to be solely answerable tti any particular club. If that were done they would bei able to bring forward and discuss reforms from an altogether unbiassed point of view and clubs from the Midlands and ,Wttls might be induced to join the Union. As constituted at present they would never induce outside clubs to seek membersh:p, and they would never do 'anything until every club had an opportunity of being represented on the committee. (Applause). In con- clusion, Mr. • Warren appealed to the players to train (hiring the summer months, and to be in form for the first match of the season, /Ind not as in the past to allow half the season to pass before they got into condition. (Applatim). During the evening the loyal and other toasts were honoured and songs were given by the players a number of whom proved themselves excellent entertainers. The "A" team have an excellent record for the season 1(305-6. They played 27 matches. of which 21 were won and three lost. They scored -12 goals, 92 tries, or 382 points, as against 15 goals 21 tries, or 102 points. Last season- 30 matches were played of which 28 were won, three lost and one drawn and 73 goals, 134 tries, or 548 points were scored as against 17 goals, 21 tries' or 103 points. The score of 318 points establishes a record. Thirty-seven players took part in Combination matches, and 42 in all matches, the object being to afford a trial to proMising juniors. In the season 1301-5 the 'A" team 44ttes were £lOO 4053.3d/over the previous season. while in 10074-0 they were .£36 in advance of any previous year. This gratifying feature, it was stated, was not alto;other due to their success ; some credit was due to the 12 a-side game. Though'some of the matches had been won by a large score, very interesting football had been shown, and in a measure went to prove' that-a reduction in the number of players, would bring about an improvement in the game. . . _ .
--Afe—dafis were presented to the following :—T. Knight (cwt.) T. Kenyon, J. Davies, G. Garside. H. Hewitt, W. Asht,on. E. Lunt, sen.' E. Lnnt, jun., W. Fairhurst, J. Lloyd, H. Forster and E. Jordan.

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.

NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Anthors of letters intended for publication must in I all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. -- Fancy Dress Parade and Carnival. Sir,—Some misunderstanding haying arisen as to where Collecting Boxes and Books for Collections before the Parade actually takes place, can be obtained, I should like to take this opportunity of informing your readers that I shall be pleased to supply an official Collecting Box to any hotel or shop-keepers who think they can help to swell the Funds. I shall also be pleased to supply any lady or gentleman who will apply to me with an official Collecting Book. I may mention that prizes will be awarded for both Box and Book collections. Thanking you in anticipation I remain yours truly, E. PICKAVANCE (Hon. Sec.)
87, Bridge st., Warrington. 14, June 1906.

Trade Union Methods. " No Good to the Painting Trade." Sir,—The value to the community, of any particular kind of labour is not to be artificially regulated either by Trades Unions or greedy employers without inter- ference with the well-being of both the employed and the community. The result in the painting and build- ing trades generally has been to throw out of employ- ment a large and steadily increasing proportion of men. These are the men who, whilst " hardy and capable looking " are for some reason not the most desirable of employees: i.e., their work does not, at Trade Union fixed wages, show a working profit to their employer. It may be no fault of their own at all, for all men are not equally efficient. This state of affairs is largely due to the Trades Union method of deciding upon what shall be called a minimum rate of wage, and failing to regulate and classify the grade of efficiency that this wage is to be paid for. Trades Unions naturally bring pressure to bear when likely to be most effective, and so obtain advances of wage. They secure the highest rate that can be obtained under the most fortuitious circumstances, and they forthwith label it" minimum rate of wage." They jail altogether in the correlative duty of guaranteeing a certain efficiency for the wage conceded. Asa matter of fact, the wage obtained is a maximum wage for the best men, and employers who pay the wage inevitably lose the difference on their contracts. The natural results are :—First, that men a little below the best in age or expertness are only employed under compulsion. Second, that men of extra capability are handicapped and unable to assert their claim to a higher remunera- tion than the general body of workers in proportion to their capacity. A third and consequent result is that the incentive to good work and self-improvement is removed, and the efficiency of the workers in the trade falls materially. The writer could give numerous inci- dents from personal knowledge of cases in which men have been six and eight months out of employment at Bd. per hour simply because, compared to others, they were not worth more than Td. A partial cure is to be found in -the fixing of a maximum and minimum wage, with a proper classification of workers according to their ability. This would offer strong inducement for personal improvement, and consequently higher qualification on the part of workers and competition among employers for the best men, who would gradually migrate to the best shops, which would then have a claim to higher charges for better class of work. It would in time do much to stop reckless competition as employers paying the highest rates would have a substantial argument , against being compared in estimating with shops employing inferior labour. In fact it would be a frank acknowledgement that all men are not equal and are not necessarily required to be,either in skill or physiane. ' Before Trades Unionism the difference in pay of he • various men employed in a decorator's shop ranged from £3 to 225. per week. At the present time in a similar shop the wages run from 455. to 365. Bd. In both cases the manager or foreman's wage is omitted no it is obvious that the levelling up has also brought, about a levelling down. In another establishment only five years ago, ten were paid Bd., two at 7c1., one at 6d., two at 10d., one at lid., and one at Is. per hour, the union served notice of Bd., as a minimum. After a long fight 81d. was conceded. The shop now pays 15 at Si. and two at Pd. There is much less esprit de corps and efficiency among the men and much less work turned out than formerly, whilst incidentally a rapidly increasing • trade which was almost now has been driven to a town miles away where wages are 7d. per hour, and the union • powerless. Trades Unions claim to have raised wages. Person- &ally I believe the rise in wages and in the purchasing power of money to be due to quite independent causes, and that the only real result has been the increased -remuneration of the undeserving at the expense of the best workmen in the community, and the undermining and destruction of that pride in skill that was at the foundation of our manufacturing and other industries. As far as Trades Unionism and the painting trade is concerned, it appears to me to have done no good to the trade as a whole. It has proved to be the worst form of protection—the protection of the lazy, the unworthy ..and incompetent, at the expense of the diligent and skilful. Since its inception workmanship has deterio- rated, apprenticeship has become almost extinct much work, such as signwriting, stencilling of friezes,decora- tion of relief, &c.—has been driven from the trade, and is accomplished by boys and girls, and it has fostered -the adoption of an enormous number of materials which ,save painters labour. As far as I can see,the percentage of these unemployed will increase annually unless these Trades Unions see lit to modify their present attitude and methods, or the workers deliver themselves from 'this new form of bondage.—Yours faithfully, WALTER J. PEARCE (Lecturer at the Manchester Technical School).

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Rev. Dr. Mercer's Resignation. A meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was field on Wednesday, Mr. .1. Billinge presiding. There were also present :—Mrs. Clay, Mrs. Wilkinson Messrs. W. Hickman, A. J. Jolley, B. Forshaw, G. Thompson, T. H. Athcrof t, J. Payton, C. Mather, M. W. Seton, W. Flanagan, S. Sutton (assistant clerk), J. F. Awbery (master), A. Wright (superintendent of the Cottage Homes).

div.head: COTTAGE HOMES.
div.p: THE COTTAGE HOMES.

At a meeting of the Padgate Schools Committee an application for the hand to take part in the cycle parade on Jtfly 21st was acceded to. Miss Ward's resig- nation was accepted and it was decided to advertise for a successor as foster mother of number three home. The nitrates were approved. "VERY LIBERAL."

A letter was read from the Ulverston Union stating that the Guardians had with the consent of the Local Government Board, united the office of matron with that of superintendent nurse, and were wishful to appoint a charge nurse at a salary of £25 per annum, increasing £2 Itm yearly to £3O. Instead of advertising the Clerk was instructed to invite applications front nurses employed in about half-a-dozen unions. The Clerk added that be should_ be _glad if the Guardians
would pass .on the letter to the Workhouse master or
superintendent, with a request that if they had on the stall a suitable certificated nurse who might desire to have a change, she would apply on the accompanying form. _

The CLERK said it was suggested that to save the Inverston Guardinns the trouble of advertising they should take a good nurse from the Warrington Union and then the Warrington Guardians would have to advertise for a successor. Mr. ASHCROFT : They are very liberal. it was decided, that the letter should lie on the table.

s.-- V THE REFERFNCE LIBRARY. A letter was read from Mr. C. Madeley, curator and librarian,asking for a ropy of the Guardians' annual year book for the local collection in the reference library and also any back numbers which could be spared. The ASSIST INT CLERK intimated that he had acceded to the request. REV. R. MERCER' RESIGNATION.

The following letter to the clerk was read from the Rev. Dr. Mercer, who recently left Warrington to take charge of St. Panlinus' Church, Lostock Uall, near Preston :—Dear Sir, It is with regret that I resign my seat on the Warrington Board of Guardians. My removal of COIItSP, makes it impossible for me to take part in those genial meetings which T have been privi- leged to share during the past couple of years. I feel that I_ owe much to yourself and beg to thank you for
• many kindly acts. The CiIAIRMAN said he had received a similar letter ' in abich Dr. Mercer expressed .the pleasure it had

Wifi;r-d-e.cr him to be associated with his colleagues—in-- the all-important work of Poor Law administration and desired him (the chairman) to convey to the Board his thanks for their valuable assistance. He also desired particularly to thank Mr. and Mrs. Awbery and Mr. and Mrs. Wright for the help they had given him in discharg- ing'his duties. The Chairman said he was sure they all regretted that it had become necessary for Dr. Mercer to resign. (Hear, hear). Mr. THOMPSON said Dr. Mercer was a very valuable member and did all the work he possibly could. He was conscientious in everything he did or said. Mr. Thompson moved a resolntion expressing regret at Dr. Mercer's severance from the Board. Mr.AsHcaorr seconded and the motion was agreed to. A LONDON CONFERENCE. QCESTIONS AFFECTING CHILDREN.

The CHAIRMAN presented an interesting report of the proceedings at a conference held in London to con- sider legislation affecting ehildren. The Warrington Board was reoresented by the Chairman, Mrs. Clay, Mr. Mather and the Clerk. Mrs. CLAY also briefly addressed the board. Mr. MATHER said the result of the conference was that it was considered inexpedient to remand juvenile offenders either to gaols or workhouses, and there was en almost unanimous opinion that it vvas also inexpedi- e• r to institute the free feeding of school children. Whit little food was required was better left to charitable institutions and not the State to supply.

div.head: DEATH OF ALD. JOHN ROBERTS, J.P.
div.p: DEATH OF ALD. JOHN ROBERTS, J.P.

In politics Alderman Roberts was a staunch Con- servative and an old election campaigner. He was prominently associated with both the Senior and Junior Conservative Associations, and was one who assisted in the building of the club in Sankey-street. He held several offices, including the chairmanship of the Bowl- ing Green Committee. His loss will be very keenly felt at St. Peter's Church. with which he had been connected for many years. He was one of the congregation who worshipped in the school before the present Church was erected and he was very warmly attached to the place. He held the office of Vicar's warden and the duties could not have been in better hands.

Alderman Roberts was of a kindly and genial dis- positjon, and although his style of speech was rugged,he never failed to make himself thoroughly understood. By his death Warrington has lost one who over tried to engage in good work.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

The funeral will take place to-day (Saturday) at the Cemetery at 12 0 noon. The members of the Council and Magistrates will meet at the Town Hall at 10 45 a.m. and join the cortege at the residence of the deceased, and proceed to St. Peter's Church where a service will be held, afterwards leaving for the Cemetery.

REFERENCE AT THE POLICE COURT. Before the opening of the business at the Borough Police Court this (Friday) morning, Alderman Smet- hurst (presiding magistrate) said he was sure he would only be expressing the feelinges of his fellow-magistrates when hesaid how deeply grigved they wore to hear of the death of Alderman Roberts who was present on that Bench only a week ago. He had occupied many public positions, especially in business, associated with the workingmen with whom he worked most cordially. Warrington would undoubtedly be the poorer by his death.

The Chief Constable, on behalf of the police, associ- ated himself with the expression of regret. Alderman Roberts was a member of the Watch Committee and had been his personal friend for many years. , Everyone who knew the late alderman would admit that he was a very flne'sample of the Englishman whose word was his 'bond. Mr. H. Thornton and Mr. E. A. White (acting magis- trates' clerk) also added their tributes to the good qualities of the late alderman.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH. ' Walking Day.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH. ' Walking Day.

Stockton Heath's annual children's festival was held this afternoon (Friday), and was made the occasion of a general holiday in the village. Early in the day the , climatic conditions were of a most. depressing character but fortunately there was a decided improvement towards noon. The village wore a true holiday garb, the residents generally making an admirable display of flags and bunting. Opposite St. Thomas' Church the trees were festooned with streamers and an animated spectacle was presented as the children began to assemble shortly after one o'clock. The first item on the programme was a brief service which was conducted in the Church by the Vicar the Rev. James Collins, after which the children were marshalled in processional order. They numbered, in round figures, I,ooo,and as many of them carried banner- ettes and flowers they made a brave show. Headed by the Blue Coat school band, the Vicar, and Church officers, they marched as far as Wilderspool brewery and returning to the swing bridge completed the journey round the village by way of Ellesmere-road,Lawrenson's Brow, and Whitefleld-road to Victoria Square. The I tail end of the procession was brought up by the infants who travelled in gaily decorated vehicles kindly lent for the occasion. Arrived at Victoria Square the pro- cessionists divided, the infants going to the Church Institute for tee, whilst the senior scholars proceeded to the schools where their wants were attended to. After tea the children adjourned to afield adjoining Wilder's- pool Brewery where the remainder of the day was enjoyably spent. '

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, June 16, 1906.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, June 16, 1906.
OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Services for Sunday.
Wycliffe Church, 10.30 and G. 30, Rev. John Yonge. Baptist Church, Latchford, 10.30 and 0, Rev. J. F. Matthews. Morning subject, "The secret of Jesus" ; evening subject The devil in bondage." _

Bews-ey-ro'ad Wesleyan Church. 10.30, Rev. S. Pitt ; 6.30, Rev. A. C. Parker. Bold-street Wesleyan Church, 10.30,Rev. John Gunnell; 6.30, Rev. S. Pitt. The annual summer services in connection with Hill Cliffe Baptist Church will be held on Sunday when the preacher will be the Rev. T. Witton Davies, Bangor University. Special music will be rendered by the choir, and solos by Miss Pattie May Roberts,Liverpool. A children's service will be held in the morning. Choir Anniversary.

The annual choir services in connection with the Latchford Baptist Church were held on Sunday when the preacher was the Rev. J. F. Matthews whose dis- courses were listened to with considerable interest. Mr. Peter Harrison was at the organ, and the conductor was Mr. W. T. Wilkinson. The choir ably contributed an anthem at each service. The offertory for the fund reached £4.

div.head: Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church.

The preacher at this church 'on Sunday morning was the Rev. T. Glading, of Bradford, who took for his text the words: "Your heavenly Father" and delivered a powerful discourse. He also made an inter- esting departure by giving a short but very interesting address to the children at one stage of the service. In the evening the Rev. W. Mellor preached, his text being : " For now we see through a glass darkly ; but then face to face ; now I know in part, but then shall I know even as also lam known."

div.head: Free Church Council.
div.p: Free Church Council.

This Council is making arrangements to hold a series of open-air services in the town during the summer months and the venture is being taken up with con- siderable enthusiasm. A preliminary meeting was held at Bold-street Church on Monday evening and it was decided to inaugurate the services with a large open- air meeting on the Fair Ground, Queen-street, on Sun- day evening, the 24th inst. Representatives of all the Nonconformist bodies will take part. Mr. C. E. Parker will preside. The speakers are the Rev. Sydney Pitt and the Rev. John Francis Matthews. The band of the Legh-street Church will lead the singing. The subse- quent meetings are to be held on Sunday evenings, at eight o'clock, in six different centres. By the kindness of the President, 2,000 copies of the Free Church Mission Hymnal have been presented for the use of the various church groups uniting in the work.

div.head: Wyciffe P.S.A.
div.p: Wyciffe P.S.A.

The usual meeting was held on Sunday, when Mr. Hilton presided and spoke upon the "Sweating system: Its evils and cruelty." He said it was the duty of all to do their utmost to discourage and as far as it was possible not to buy articles made under such conditions. Mr. Lightspoke on Job's declaration " f shall see God." When we looked upon the works of art, he said, we wished to see the artist. When we read the works of a great mind our desire was to see the author. So with great men as we read of them, we admire their words, but we longed to see the man. God was the maker of beautiful lives, and beautiful characters and we longed to see him. We are confident that bye and bye we shall see God's face. The secretary heartily welcomed two new members, (total 158) and asked the members to put all the enthusiasm possible into the renovation scheme. Mr. Hilton recited "The old clock on the stairs," in a masterly style which was appreciated by the brethren. The secretary led the prayer and read the lesson. Thirty shillings was collected for the first Sunday towards the £lOO for the repairing of the organ and its improvements. Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac., presided at the organ.

Presbyterian Anniversary. The anniversary services in connection with St. John's Presbyterian Church were held on Sunday when the Rev. Thomas Mackay, of Pendleton, preached morning and evening. Th the afternoon at 9.30 a service of song, entitled " Gems from the life of Isaac Marsden," was given by the choir. Mr. J. W—lowett presided at the organ, Miss McLeod giving the connec- tive readings. There were good attendances at all the services, especially in the evening when Mr. Mac Kay preached from the word," Then said He unto me, Son of man, hast thou seen what the ancients for the house of Israel do in the dark, every man in the chamber of his imagery ? for they say, the Lord seeth irs not ; the Lord bath I forsaken the earth." No wonder, said the preacher, that Ezekiel was staggered by what he i saw n these chambers of imagery, because what he saw was not evil doubly distilled but evil twelve-fold distilled. There had been open and pubilc idolatry in Jerusalem, but, such was the downward and debasing tendency of evil, that it seemed not sufficient for these men to have public and established idolatry. Apart from the evil that might be done in the broad daylight something must be dono in the dark—in concealment—blacattse when wickedness could be done in public it ceased ts he enjoyable. It was stolen waters that were sweet. The mind of man was a chamber of imagery in whose darkness work went on hidden from the world. The chamber of immagery was the test of their character. A man was precisely what he was in the dark—no one was better than his secrets. Their imagination had a tremendous influence on their life, and it was important that it should be pure and sanctified. Let them guard their imagination, watch their thoughts. and seek to have a pure mind and a pure heart. Special hymns Were sung, and at the evening service the choir gave a rendering of the anthem " What are these ?" (Mellor), the solo part being taken by the Misses Ditchfleld and Dewar. Satisfactory collections were obtained towards the church fund.

div.head: WHO LED? -- Controversy Over Municipal Free
div.p: WHO LED? -- Controversy Over Municipal Free
Libraries.
WARRINGTON'S UNDOUBTED CLAIM.

Manchester and Liveipool are at present engaged in acontroversey as to which city was the pioneer in the establishment of free libraries, and in the discussion Warrington's undoubted claims to that honour are being entirely ignored. It would be us well to remind the inhabitants of these two great cities that however they may regard Warrington's lack of progress in the past, in respect to free libraries they followed the lead of the town of many industries. Seen yesterday, Alderman Bennett, whose interest in the subject is second to none, had no hesitation in say- ing, and saying most emphatically, that Warrington was undoubtedly Ail° first town to avail itself of the Act of Parliament which empowered municipal bodies to pro- vide free libraries out of the rates. He could not under- stand on what Manchester based its claim and he regarded Liverpool, so to speak. as being altogether out of the running. Neither, he assured us, was entitled to the honour.

Warrington's position has been seriously assailed by Salford but it has been proved that Warrington's library was established in 1819, whilst Salford did not I move in the matter until a year later. It is a fact that Salford was the first to allow borrowers to take books to their homes, whilst Warrington only threw open its liberary to those who came to consult it on the spot but this is only a question of degree and does not invalidate Warrington's claims to be the pioneer. As "The Dawn "said on a recent accasion, "It may restrict our laurels, but it certainly can not displace them."

REFORMED EPISCOPAL CHURCH. General Synod at Warrington. During the week the annual synod in connection with the Reformed Episcopal Church has been held at War- rington. The proceedings opened on Monday eveninr, when a special service was held in Emmanuel Church, Bold-street. There was a fairly large congregation. The preacher was the Rev. HERRIES GanGonY,M.A., who took for his text "Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular," I. Corinthians xii., 27. During the course of his sermon, the rev. gentleman said that, as a stranger amongst them, he asked themall to surrender themselves to Christ as they were. If an individual member of the Church was out of touch with God, then the whole of the congregation suffered. The Church was losing ground because the individual mem- bers were losing sight of the fact that Christ was the head,and that they were the body. All their food passed to them spiritually through Christ. If one led an un-Christian life,then the.whole body of Christ suffered. If they were not consecrated to Christ, they would go along the downward path, but if they were consecrated to Him, and humbly and prayerfully fought for Him, their path would be upwards. The nearer each one of them got to God, the nearer would all the people be together...
Then followed a celebration of the Holy Communion the Right Rev. Bishop Eldridge officiating, and special hymns were sung._

0- PUBLIC MEETING. On Tuesday evening a well-attended public meeting was held in the Emmanuel Church Institute, Knutsford- road. Commander Robinson, R.N., presided and was supported amongst others by the Right Rev. Bishop Eldridge, D.D. The C lIA [IIMAX, in a brief address, saidhe was driven out of the Church of England because of its tendency in the direction of Rome. It was on the road to Rome and would not stop until the peaple of the country opposed its progress in that direction by all the means in their power. When they looked at the controversy over the Education Bill they saw a Bishop of the Established Church saying that simple Bible teaching meant death to all Christianity, and another Bishop openly advocating an alliance with the Roman Catholic Church to oppose Bible teaching which was without their dogmas, doctrines and Romish teachings. When they saw that was it not time to consider whether they were not justified in bringing their children into the Reformed Episcopal Church? THE REFORMED EPISCOPAL CHURCH. • -

Addresses were then delivered upon the Reformed EPiscopal Church. Speaking on " Its Episcopal Origin and Orders" the Rev. Dr. BOWMAN said that many years before the Reformed Episcopal Church sprang into existence evangelical Churchmen were justly alarmed at the steady progress of sacerdotal principles and ritualistic practices in the Established Church. Long before the least suspicion of any definite purpose for a union with the Church of Rome was entertained,the Rofnish atmosphere which had been created in the Church was causing many in high official positions to view the movement with suspicion and dismay,and their founders met together and decided to embark upon the momentous enterprise and to strike for truth and free- dom. Since the Reformed Episcopal Church was launched it had passed through many storms but the old ship was still seaworthy and could not founder so long as the old flag of the Gospel was above it. (Rear hear.) It might ba doubted whether the orders of their Church were valid—thev claimed to possess equally with the Church of England, anything which was valid in Episcopal orders—and they regarded its episcopal quality as a valuable asset, but whilst the oreers were essential to its wel- fare they were not essential to its being. They ' did not claim Apostolic succession, believing that the true test of the minister was that he should possess spiritual gifts to testify to the end that in the Gospel and the Gospel alone was the power of salvation to everyone who believed. (Applause.) The Rev. T. HEATH delivered an address on "Its liturgical worship." Of the methods of conducting I service, he said, he claimed that the liturgical was the best as he believed that there should be an agreement between the minister and his people. The liturgy provided against omissions in prayer, but perhaps its greatest claim lay in the responses. There was no doubt that it was an instinct of the religious heart to make audible assent to supplications on its own behalf. They claimed for the liturgy of the Reformed Episcopal Church that it had been purged of what an evangelical clergyman had called pegs on which to hang Popery, and that from it had been expunged all that savoured of sacerdotalisni. Upon them rested the responsibility of maintaining what they believed tube one of if not abso- lutely the purest and most beautifullittrgieisipionn ,e.xTishte- enco. (Applause). protestant The R e v evangelicalSGr' 7: u°l‘trentel speakings of our Reformed Episcopal Church," said he would endeavour to draw a contrast between that which they professed and the heresies practiced by ritualists which had called their Church into existence. It was not the Church of Rome which led to the formation of the Reformed Episcopal Church hut the perversion of the Church of England in the direction of Rome. The rev, gentleman proceeded to instance practices and doctrines of the Church of England against which they protested and which they rejected. What had caused him to leave the Church of England, of which at one time he was a clorgyman,waa the doctrine of regeneration in baptism. They pro- tested against those things and against the growing prevalence of blasphemies which had called them into existence, and believed that the greatest of evangelical doctrines d m. trainnesnwasnth(lpCptilralisistew)as the one mediator between G The Rev. S. Nmstr, M.A., read a paper on "The Catholic platform of the Reformed Episcopal Church." Their position, he said, was of the oneness or unity of all Christians throughout the world. For their Roman Catholic friends they had a deep regard and concern,' but they could not allow that the Church of Rome was ' the one Church of Christ, and from that they con- scientiously and strongly dissented. They must resist all attempts by Rornanisers to bring their children under the Pope. He never heard anything so terrible in his life as the horrible blasphemy that God had written a book which could not I teach what He wanted to teach, but that some priestly hireling, some wonderful high priest of to-day, was to say what must be left out of the Bible and what was essential. Let them do their utmost to dispel the darkness of suspicion and priestcraft which was gather- ing round their children by opening the doors and pouring forth a flood of light. The unity of all Christians was an essential part of their creed but were they not in danger from that which they deplored in others ? He had hoard Nonconformist adherents of their Church spoken of as if they were different and of lower caste, as though they were/not all brethren, all children of one common Father. He appealed to them to have done with the childish fault of branding those who did not entirely fall in with them. The only test after death would bathe question" Lovest thou Me? "and if they could answer that question as Peter answered it, no matter to which section of the Church of Christ they belonged on earth, they would pass the test. To-day was not the time for standing aloof. Let all Evangelical Churches, liturgical or non-liturgical, unite end the battle would be won, but let them be shy, stiff, self satisfied, caring for each rift which divided them and the enemy would be strengthened and would be success- ful. (Applause). Votes of thanks to the Chairman and speakers con- cluded the meeting.

div.head: CROSFIELD'S RECREATION GROUND. To be Opened by-11-451. CrosfieidlM.P.
div.p: CROSFIELD'S RECREATION GROUND. To be Opened by-11-451. CrosfieidlM.P.

This (Saturday) afternoon the recreation ground in Hood-lane which has been acquired by the employs of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Limited, will be formally opened by Mr. A. IL Crosfield, M.P. The pro- ceedings will be of a very• interesting character. The employSs will assemble at the works at two o'clock when a procession will be formed including the works' hand, the fire brigade, and the ambulance corps. On arrival at Hood-lane at 2.30. Mr. A. FL Crosfleld will declare the ground open. Dr. Markel and Mr. Henry Roberts will subsequently open play on the bowling green, Mr. J. 3. Cresfteld will bowl the first ball on the cricket ground, while the tennis court will be opened by Captain U. 1. Crosfieid. A few particulars of the recreation scheme in con- nection with the firm will doubtless be of interest. It is a condition of employment that each person shall contribute one penny per week to a Recreation Fund. The rule was at first confined to the workpeople and was suggested by them with the view of providing a Recreation Ground for the cricket, football,athletic and bowling sections of the old Athletic Club, as well as other means of rational amusement and social and physical recreation. Later, the offices and chemical laboratory entered into the scheme. Thus every employs by virtue of his contribution is a member of the Recreation Club. The fund is controlled by the Works Council, a body representative of all departments whose functions are in the main advisory but which in this matter acts as trustee in the interests of the work- people, It is a general direction to this Council that it may Make appropriations in aid of "any scheme devised to engage the leisure activities of the employs le a wholesome pursuit, pastime or hobby, or in work for the good of the community." Under these wide terms of reference it will be seen that every form of social activity is eligible for support • sections with objects so diverse as those of Football and Ambulance being associated in one organisation. The object is to wele all the institutions together and an to infuse a spirit of loyal co-operation. Even societies which are financially self-contained are con- sequently required to be affiliated to the club. Besides committees for the various sections there is an Execu- tive Committee for general purposes, which has charge of the new Recreation ground. This ground is ten acres in extent and comprises within its area bowling green, cricket field and cycle track, croquet lawns, lawn tennis courts, hockey and football fields, and a full equipment for the various games, completed by a splcndid pavilion. Admission to the groundwill be free to all employjs and visitors will be admitted at a charge of Id. each, if accompanied by a member tr., members.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby, Football. By " Ovalist"

Just for one week, football takes the first place in public interpst again. The annual meeting of the Northern Union was held on Tuesday, and such changes in the rules of the game were made as may have an important bearing on the future of the Northern Union. The most drastic change was that propokd by the Warrington Club and supported by Leigh, that the number of players be thirteen a side. When I saw from the agenda of business that War- rington had made this proposition I had little hope of seeing it carried, notwithstanding the great success which twelve a aide football among the " A " and junior teams has proved. I am unfeignedly glad, however, that the change has come about. Many of my readers will doubtless remember that I advanced the thirteen a side suggestion in this column a couple of seasons ago as being the most practical one for open- ing out the game and making it better from a specta- torial point of view. Thirteen seems to me to be the ideal number—six forwards, two halves, four threes, and one full back—and it is a matter for increased satisfaction that the change has come about through the instrumentality of the Warrington Club.

Other important changes have also been made in the playing rules. The one affecting touch play bids fair to settle a vexed question. In future deliberate kicking to touch, except in the case of a penalty, will gain no ground. The ball will simply be brought back and scrummaged. When carried into touch the usual " scrum "opposite the point of entry into touch will follow. This is an alteration which should do much to lessen monotonous touch play and incessant scrummaging.

The third and last change is also of considerable importance, but as to its wisdom lam in some doubt. In effect it is a return to the Rugby Union " play the ball "rule, and makes it imperative for a player when tackled to at once put the ball down in front of him and between himself and his opponents' goal-line. The game should be quickened thereby, and the number of stoppages and scrummages reduced still further. Other complications, and possibly injuries to players who are averse to parting with the ball near their own goal-line, may ensue. Anyhow the experiment—which is not a blind one of course,—is worth a trial.

Generally speaking the changes are the most important which have taken place since the formation of the Union. The decline in popularity of the game rendered drastic reforms imperative, and the Union is to be complimented on having boldly faced the future and made a strong endeavour to win back public favour. Next season the games will certainly be faster, more open, and more scientific. Pace and com- bination will be more•essential than ever, and in view of Warrington's failure in the past, strict training must be the order of the day. Under the new rules the team which does not train and practice assiduously will soon be outclassed. Warrington %light to do well if the training difficulty can be overc'ome. We have the men here who can play the open game as well almost as any club in the Union, and they will get more scope than heretofore.

The section of the team most affected by the changes will be the forward division with their mem- bers reduced to six. The scrummagers will require more careful selection. The standard of forward play will most certainly become higher. A man, to be a good forward under the new rules, will need something more than avoirdupois and pushing ability. He must be able to run and handie the Will with some skill as well. Mere weight will be less esseintial —speed and cleverness a sine qua non. Luckily the Warring- ton Club is well-off forwar3, and six of the best ' should be available at all times. . I foresee the neces- sity for new blood behind. A new right wing of pace and dash will be indispensable, and the sooner he is found and the better. Fish, if in condition, should have the best time of his life under the new rules. Space will be more plentiful, and opportunities for scoring multiplied considerably. Now then, Warring- ton ! Up with the primrose and blue right to the top ! !

Cricket. Warrington are going strong for thie West Lancashire League G`bamplonship—althongh it is rather early in the season to say so. They have got together a power- ful eleven and on present form should be ecinal to any club in the League. On Saturday they made short work of Prescot who are looked upon as one of the best teams in the district. The afternoon was on ideal one for the summer sport and there was an encouraging attendance. Warrington went to the wicket first and the feature of the innings was the fine display of J. W. Bibby whose turn came at a critical period of the game.He at once hit out freely and soon improved the aspect of affairs for War- rington, making 31 before he was caught by Holden. The tail of the eleven wagged strongly, with the result that the Warringtonians amassed 157. J. Cresswell, the professional, and J. Thompson were both in grand form and made 23 and 25 respectively.

The visitors did not give much troubJe, and were all dismissed for GO. Cresswell worked great havoc with the ball, capturing six wickets for 20 runs. This is the first time this season that he as had the advantage of operating on a dry wicket, and as a fast bowler proved a great success. He maintained a good length throughout and conipelled the batsmen to act largely on the defensive. Connor also did accept- able work, his analysis working out at three wickets for 39 runs, while Duckworth kept wicket in splendid style. The home fielders were also on the alert and missed very few chances.

'The second eleven were not so fortunate in their match at Prescot, being defeated by a margin of 2G. No fewer than four players were out for lbw, and the accuracy of the decisions was much questioned by the visitors. The top scorer for Warnngton was T. Houghton who made 15. Bennett howled very effectively and secured eight wickets for 65 runs.

- Sankey Wire Mills entertained Frodsham and were lucky in making a draw. The visitors having made 142 for four wickets thought it safe to declare and the Wire Mills had responded with 55 for 7 when the time limit was reached. Ferguson batted in grand style for the villagers and made 49, 'l. Whitfield (13 not out) giving the best display for the Wire Mills?
By a margin of 2 Latchford Baptists 2nd triumphed over St. James's, their top scorer being J. Sherratt who made 23.

Moore and Daresbury experienced a pretty severe drubbing at Weaverharn where the home team ran up a majority of 52. %V. Johnson was a host in himself, his innings realizing. 3 while his bowling achievement was two wickets for 24 runs.

- ------ Grapnenhall defeated Glazebury by 22, while Oughtrington Park were beaten by Llanwrst in no half- hearted style. No doubt the outing to the charming %Vet's-5 resort compensated for the disappoinments of the game.
Ellesmere-street Wesleyans 'were victorious over Widnes St. Mary's 2nd, J, Allen (17) being the top scorer.
Cheshire Lines Engineers were beaten by I atchford Baptists who ran up 69 as compares! with their M. R. Byrne (16) was the most successful batsman.
Bewsey Wesleyans easily accounted for Rylands' recreation who gave a very tame display. For the victors Jolley captured 5 wickets for 10 runs and Millett 4 for 19 runs.

Considerable interest is being taken in the works competition. On Friday evening Monks, Hall and Co. passed a total of 53, scored by R. A. Naylor's with 8 wickets in band and on Tuesday Richmonds' had the best of the match with L. and N.-W. Railway.

The first round of the Works Squadron Championship was entered upon on Thursday evening before a large attendance at the Legh Streetl baths. Six teams should have met but only one race was actually decided, Whitecross and Sankey Wire Mills both failed to put in an appearance and were disqualified. The contest between :Post Offiice and Pearson and Knowles was postponed for a week. The teams which met were Richmond's and Ryland'. The two first men got off the mark well together but the Richmond's man was quickly left behind, losing several yards. The deficiency wa.s worked off by G. Anderton and in the end Richmond's won a bard race by two yards. Time 2 mins 44 secs.

Thursday's programme included a water polo match in connection with the second division of the Liverpool and District League, the teams being Warrington and Souti. Hill. Before the match the plaNers indulged in a squadron race which was won by Warrington by a foot after they had led by half-a-dozen yards.
In the that half of the match Warrington de- fended the shallow end. South Hill attacked and

Woods just managed to tip a shot by White round the post, only to be beaten by the same player a few seconds later. Re-starting Ashton put in some excellent work and passed to Boscow who sent in a hard shot. It however, lay to Ashton to equalize with a shot from half way which completely beat Foster. Allen next had an excellent opening a minute later but was too slow to take advantage of it. Frost, immediately afterwards spoiled a fine effort, by shooting wide after taking the ball half the length of the bath.

Ewhange'play followed when the ball was passel to Boscow whohad a clear field and scored. Frost immediately equalized. South Hill were having rather the best of matters bq their shooting was rather wild. They were attacking when the ball was passed to Ashton who scored with a shot almost the whole length of the bath. Half time arrived with Warrington leading by 3 goals to 2.

The early part of the second half was marred by a succession of fouls given against Warrington. Ashton and Boscow both had hard luck in hitting the crossbar, especially as Aird equalised after some loose work and the match ended in a draw. Ashton for Warrington was the best player in the bath and had it not been for really splendid work by Foster would have given War- rington the lead.
On the form which they showed Warrington should next Thursday defeat Salford in the first round for the Lancashire county championship cup.
Cycling.

The weather was ideal for cycling on Saturday and followers of the pastime were out in strong forgo. The Warrington Club went to Siddington and the run to that picturesque village was thoroughly enjoyed.

On Tuesday evening Little Leigh was visited and on ' Wednesday the bowling handicap for the silver cup presented by the late Mr. George Watkins was resumed at Sankey Chapel House. This event is arousing great interest and a keen contest is anticipated.

div.p: BEAUTIFUL WARRINGTON 'SOCIETY.

Eat something with currants in it. Currants are amongst the cheapest and most valuable things you can use. They are nearly all actual nourishment. The King's doctor recommends currant bread as a palatable, wholesome food, which is in itself a sufficient diet. Ask your baker for White or Hans currant bread and get him to supply it regularly.

MEETING OF THE GENERAL COMAITTEE.

A meeting of the General Committee of the Beautiful Virarrington Society was hold at the Old Academy on Tuesday evening. Reports from the ward secretaries were received, all indicating that the work was pro- gresAng satisfactorily. A report from the Show Com- mittee was also considered, and it was decided definitely to hold the show on September Ist. The place has not yet bleu settled, hut it is hoped that the Park Recrea- tion Ground will be available.

div.head: TOWN HALL WARD.
div.p: TOWN HALL WARD.

A meeting of the Town Hall Ward Committee of the Society was held in the Kendrick-street Schools on Wednesday evening at S o'clock the chair being taken by Alderman Smethurst and there were also present, Ciptain Crosfield, Messrs. Page, Fern, Cowdelt, Mrs. Smethurst and Miss Birchall.

The Chairman and Utptain Cro-s-field both commented upon the good work the Society was doing in the Town. Many suggestions as to the mode of working were discussed and a letter was read from Dr. Markel with respect to the proposed planting of trees in eligible streets, and certain proposals were made to be laid before the Executive Committee for their con- sideration. The committee meet on the third Wednes- day of the month to discuss and to note the progress of the work for the ward. THE ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual Tneetinz of the Society will be held in the Parr flail on Wednesday evening. After the transaction of routine business addresses will be de- livered by iqr. Owen Greening, of London, Rev. Canon Stevenson and others. The public are requested to attend in large numbers and show their interest in the movement. _ _
At a meeting of the Latchford Ward Committee, a scheme was (4)nsicired for canvassing the ward in order to secure n full attendance of members at the Society's annual meeting.

div.head: NEW LIFE-BOAT.
div.p: A NEW LIFE-BOAT.

The Royal National Life-Boat institution has sent to Hoylake a new Life-BoAt to replace the boat stationed there by the Institution many years ago. The new boat, which was built by the Thames Ironworks Company, is of the" Liverpool " type, 38ft. long by lOft, wide, rows 12 oars, and is fitted with two drop keels and two water- ballast tanks. A new transporting carriage, fitted with Tipping's plaDmvays, has been provided &ir use with the new Life-Boat, in order that she may be readily trans- ported over the beach to the spot nearest to the scene of the wreck requiring her assistance. The boat is named the "Hannah Fawsett Bennett," her cost having been partially defrayed from the bequest to the Institu- tion of the late Mrs. Bennett, of Florence. The Com- mittee of Management are much indebted to the Local Committee, and to Mr. W. B. Charles, the honorary secretary, for their valnahle co-operation in the manage- ment of the Hoylake Life-Boat Station. The Royal National Life-Boat Institution has now 231 Life-Boats under its management, and the total number of lives for the saving of which it has granted rewards since its establishment in 1824 has been 15,776. div.head: WARRINGTON HORSE PARADE. A CREDITABLE DISPLAY.
div.p: WARRINGTON HORSE PARADE. A CREDITABLE DISPLAY.

It was as a May celebration that Warrington's annual horse parade was originally ,organized. But the" merrie " month of which poets sing is oftener than not marked by fickleness of. climate, and the success of one or two parades ;has, from the spec- tacular standpoint, been marred by rain. June is now the month which finds favour for the holding of the procession, and the wisdom of the choice of date could not have been better illustrated than on Saturday when the sixth annual parade took place under ideal conditions. Throughout the day there was resplendent sunshine from an almost cloudless sky, end the Committee had indeed reason to congratulate themselves upon the complete success which crowned their efforts. The show was in every way worthy of a busy industrial town. There was a grand array of horses and it was clearly evident that the great object of the parade— to induce drivers to take the best possible care of their charges—is being achieved. Without exception the horses were in fine condition and well-groomed. While the entries were about the same as last year, there was a distinct advance in quality and the task of the judges, in awarding the prizes, was by no means easy. Their decisions, however, appeared to give satisfaction. The judging took place on Arpley fields and among the interested 1 spectators were Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., (president) and Lady preenall who have all along done their utmost to promote the success of these parades. When the judging had been completed, Lady Greenall presented the cups, medals and diplomas to the winners. It should be mentioned that every com- petitor who carried off a first prize also received a diploma presented by the R S.P.C.A. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Lady Greenall on the pro- position of Mr. Robert Pierpoint, seconded by Mr. W. Fletcher. In responding, Sir Gilbert Greenall said that anyone who had seen the horses shown that day must have been impressed with the improvement on previous parades and one thing which had improved more than anything else was the shoeing of the horses. The procession then left the ground and paraded the principal streets of the town. Heading it was the Corporation Fire Brigate• (in charge of Superintendent Turner) with gaily decorated engines, and the firemen looked smart in their bright helmets. The Volunteer transports (in charge of Sergeant Simpson) and the Police Ambulance folloWed. Then came Walker's band discoursing lively music and preceding the splendid teams of heavy horses belonging to that firm. Messrs. Greenall Whitley and. Co.'s Fire Brigade, under Snpertendent Ince, added another touch of variety to the procession, and this company's powerful horses also excited general admiration. A particularly fine animal was the one wh'cla carried off the cup for the best heavy horse. There was a long line of gaily-caparisondd horses and turnouts of all des- criptions, which reflected credit on our local trades- people,. More music was provided by the Borough Band. The only fault which could be found with the procession—as has been pointed out on previous occasions—was the lack of novelty. From the spectators' standpoint, the effect would be much improved if one or two original features could be introduced for, creditable is the display undoubtedly is, it becomes somewhat monotonous to the average onlooker who is not particularly interested in horse- flesh. Accompanying the procession was a great army of collectors on behalf of the Infirmary and District Nursing Association who reaped a rich harvest. Alderman Roberts (chairman) and several members of the Workingmen's Committee rode in an open carriage. The arrangements had been admirably carried out by the following committee :—Messrs. %V. Bainbridge, H. Ferguson, jun., W. Fletcher, Rol?ert Garton, S. Pickton, H. G. Roberts, %V. P. Rylands, R. Span; George Venn. The duties of judges were discharged by Messrs. John. Abbott, Thomas Baxter, P. Davies, William Fairclough, Peter Knowles, John Longshaw, George Marsh, Thomas Percival, N. Pilling, E. W. Sankey, Robert 3i'urner, J Turton, W. Gilbert, James Gould, Special praise is due to the hon. secretary (Mr. A. H. Clive) and the bon treasurer (Mr. J. Fulton Smith) for. their valuable services.

The other officials were T. H. Petty, chief marslaal ; Mr. Herbert Burrows, assistant marshal ; Mr. I Peter Davies, referee; and stewards, Messrs. W. P. Rylands, R. 'Spann, W. Bainbridge, W. Fletcher, W. Tinsley, Robert Garton, S. Piekton, M. G. Roberts and H. Ferguson. The stewards for non-competitors were Messrs. H. G. Roberta and S. nekton.

The "motor throat" has at last come. We have been expecting it for some time. A Manchester surgeon is reported as having spoken very seriously about throat affections set up by the irritation of dust. Bacilli of tuberculosis and other diseases are whirled about from place to place with most alarming possibili- ties for the human race. In this case, however, the motorist who kicks up the dust is as much exposed to the dangers as is the suffering pedestrian. As a display of horse flesh, Saturday's Horse Parade was a grand success. We do hope, however, that next year there will be some attempt at the intro- duction of novelty in the procession. The man in the street finds it hard to wax enthusiastic on the merits of horses in never-ending succession—splendid speci- mens though they may be—and the parade would gain much in attractiveness and there would be a greater incentive to generosity on behalf of the local charities if serious attention were paid to the spectacular side. * * Very few Building Society's in the United Kingdom can show such a long and successful career as the Warrington Workingmen's Building Society. As will be seen from our report in another column the Society has just held its 36th annual meeting and from its , I first year to its present one its history has been onel steady progress. Several of the Managers have been connected with it for the greatest portion of the 36 years and its position redounds very much to their ' credit. The society has also proved to be of consider- able benefit to many people in the town and it has encouraged habits of thrift and enabled them to become proud possessors of their own houses. * * The recent type-writing feat of a young man in the , United States is truly amazing as an example of digital dexterity. In sixty-two seconds he succeeded in writing, without a single mistake, no fewer than 230 words of connected prose. This means that in one minute he wrote 222 words. Further analysis shows that to make these words entailed his depressing the keys of the machine 1,077 times. If an ordinary person tries to tap on a table seven times in a second he will not be able to keep up that rate of speed very long. But this young man was not only tapping on an average seventeen times in a second,but his fingers were going in different directions, and the complex mental processes accompanying such physical actions are bewildering to imagine.

Brilliant Motor Lights. I Motorists have been accused of selfishness in using gas lamps of dazzling power, calculated to momentarily blind the approaching cyclist. On the other hand, it iserged by car-users that cyclists were the first to adopt gas lamps, and that even the candle iamps of alorse-drawn brougham produce a dazzling effect on a dark read. Moreover, for years past, the huge parcel coaches sent aldwg cer- tain main routes by the Pest .Office have carried five or six powerful lainps, it being found impos- sikkle otherwise to avoid collisions with the unlit lumbering waggons in charge of sleeping. drivers, which are too often encountered in the .country. Although-cyolists undoubtedly stiffer inconvenience when meeting brightly lighted cars, it is claimed •that it Would be unsafe for the swifter vehicles to overtake•wheelruen, whose position in the dark is difficult to discern, unless assisted by powerful headlights, and that, therefore, a two evils the lesser should be tolerated. Locating Minute Punctures. A writer on tyre' troubles recommends the fol- lowing method of discovering a leak which baffles the usual,search. If the method Of stretching the air tube under water fails to reveal the leak,' try the plan of pourinc, a little water into the tube through the valve, 'drying the tube, and inflating. If the water is now run round and round if is sure to find the hole eventually. If pressure is insuffi- cient to drive it out, with the tube out of the tyre, put it in again and pump up hard. After a few minutes the removal of the tube should find the wet leakea ont somewhere. It is not advisable to leave the water in the tube, •as it may cause trouble when the next big puncture comes along. - The Troubles of the Motor Cycliste Old cyclists who still follow the pastime can sympathize with the troubles through which the motor cyclist of to-day has to wade. In course of time the harassment caused by the wear of belts and pulleys, the ignition worries, broken pipes, &c., will be overcome, and driving a motor will become a kid-glove task. The fact that two ladies drove tri-cars from London to (.linburgh inside twenty- four hours lately ' is an augury in this direction. Constant improvementi ate being effected, just as was the case with the push bicycle in the early days when spokes broke, balls fractured, pedals came loose, and bearing's needed frequent lubrication and ad instment.

The death took place at his residence at Grappenhall on Monday night`of Mr. John Smith, the representative of the parish on the Runcorn Rural District Council and on the Run Corn Board of Guardians. The • deceased gentleman, who Was 62 years of age, had a severe stroke of paralysis late on Thursday night. Dr. Jago and Dr. Joseph were called in, but their efforts were unavailing and he passed away as stated. Mr. Smith was educated at the Warrington Blue Coat School, and some years later was appointed schoolmaster at Warburton school and choirmaster and organist af the Church. These positions he held for a.eomiderable number of years, returning a few years ago when he went to reside at Grappenhall. He had been t member of the Grappen- hall Parish Choral) for a few years. Ho was a regular worshipper at GrapPenhall Church, and was a staunch Conservative. kle leaves a widow and five children. VOTE OF CONDOLENCE. At the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians at Dutton Workhouse do Tuesday Mr. S. Woodward, who presided, referred to the loss sustained by the Board in the death of Mr. Smith. and moved a vote of condolence to the family. He Said all the mem- bers sympathized with them in their sad affliction. The resolution was seconded, and carried in silence. On the motion of Mrs Pilling (chairman), the Rural Disttict Council passed a- similar vote of condolence. GAMING AT WEST BANK. At Widnes Petty Sessions last Thursday Patrick Connolly, of Bridge.street,Edward McKay, of Muspratt- street, and James Cafferty, of Davies-street, pleaded "guilty "to a charge of having gambled on the West Bank Dock Estate on Sunday, the 27th ult.-Detective- sgeant Davinson deposed to having seen them playing "Bicker" and to having seen money change hands every time that the cards were dealt.-Replying to the Clerk (Mr. IL W. H. Thomas; he said people whose windows overlooked the spot had complained to the police. Inspector Pound stated that McKay had been eight times previously convicted, and Cafferty three times. Neither had, however, been convicted.of gaming. Nothing was known against Connolly.-McKay and Cafferty were each fined 2s. lid, and Gs. costs, Connolly beink ordered to pay costs alone. Messrs. Watts are issuing a sixpenny booklet by Mr. .Toseph McCabe on "The Truth about 'Secular Education its history and results." Commencing With the relatively wide-spread system of education which obtained under the Roman Empire, the writer passes to the almost total eclipse of popular instruction during the middle ages. He deals with the modern revival of education on a secular basis, and argues that instruction given by the State should be purely secular, fie adduces statistics to show that, contrary to some recent allegations; the results of secular education, where adopted, have been wholly hplinficial.

Another of Warrington's most useful and honoured townsmen passed away on Wednesday in the person of Alderman John Roberts, J.P. Although for some time his many friends had been much concerned about the state of his health, the end came very suddenly. He was in his place as usual at the Town Council meeting on Thursday of last week, and spoke at some length on the Corporation's recent experiment in the direct employment of labour on the painting of the markets. On Friday he delivered a speech at the annual meeting of the Conservative Association, in which he referred to electioneering experiences of bye-gone days. His last public act was in connection with the institution to which he was so deeply attached—the Warrington Infumary.Two-thirds of the collection taken during the progress of the Horse Parade on Saturday was devoted to the institu- tion and Alderman Roberts, along with other members of the Workingmen's Committee, rode in the proces- sion in an open carriage. In the evening he went to Southport for a short holiday and stayed at 26, Saunders-street. On Sunday morning he became ' seriously ill with hcemorrhage and Dr. Fenn, of South- port, and subsequently Dr. Joseph, of Warrington, were summoned. Despite their attention he became unconscious and died at 2.30 on Wednesday morning in his seventieth year. It was with deep regret that the townspeole generally heard of his death, for he was held in the highest esteem by members of all classes and parties. His career had been an interest- ing sad useful one. A native of Nantwich he early became associated with the tanning industry and successively held positions at Nantwich, Birkenhead, Tranmere, Kirkdale, Liverpool and other places. In 1866 he came to Warrington as manager for Messrs. Arthur Waring and Co., Winwick-road. He threw himself into the work with great energy and it was mostly due to his initiative and sound management that the firm made such rapid progress. Mr. Roberts ultimately- became managing director, and was a large shareholder in the concern. Unquestionably the public work which he had most at heart was that of furthering the interests of the Infirmary of which he was never tired of expressing his warmest admiration. Ever since the formation of the Workingmen's Committee twenty-six years ago he had occupied the chairman- ship and he rendered most devoted and ungrudging service to the organization. Under his leadership the committee has become a great power in the raising of funds from the workingmen on behalf of the Infirm- ary and at every annual meeting he had words of con- gratulation and encouragement for the workers. It was his particular ambition that the committee should subscribe £l,OOO annually and only at the last annual gathering he noted with pleasure that they were approaching very near to the attainment of that object. He was a life governer of the Infirmary and a member of the Finance and Visiting Com- mittees, and of the Board of Management and took a keen interest in their work. It was in 1897 after a contest that he entered the Town Council as representative of St. John's Ward and he remained a member up to the time of his death. Only on the Gth February of this year he succeeded to the aldermanio seat formerly held by the late Alderman Hutchinson. The other candidate was Councillor Ellison who received ten votes as against 17 recorded for Mr. Roberts. After the Note had been taken the new alder- man cordially shook hands with his opponent and in a short speech expressed his good feeling towards him and his pride at becoming an alderman. Alderman Roberts was a conscientious and hard working councillor and was a member of the Watch, Town Hall, Parks and Baths, Gas, Water and General Purposes 'Committees, deputy chairman of the Paving and Sewerage Committee and chairman of the Markets Committee. He was appointed justice of the peace for the Borough by the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster in 1900 and was regular in his attendance at the Court.
